mistakes.text: Writing [2, inf]. Always write [2, inf).

Writing (3, 1) for "from 3 down to 1"; the
  smaller number goes first: (1, 3).

- |a + b| is NOT |a| + |b| in general (see triangle inequality).
   - |-x| = |x|, but "-|x|" is always <= 0. Do not confuse them.

- Forgetting to FLIP the inequality when multiplying/dividing by a
     negative number.
   - Writing |x| > 3 as -3 > x > 3 (impossible). Correct: x < -3 OR x > 3.
   - Treating "OR" as "AND" (intersection vs union).

assuming equality. J. Related: Cauchy-Schwarz and vector
   norms (Module 10), error bounds in numerical analysis.

- (a+b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 (WRONG; correct: a^2 + 2ab + b^2).
   - 2^3 * 3^3 = 6^6 (WRONG). Different bases do not combine: 2^3*3^3 =
     (2*3)^3 = 216.
   - a^m + a^n = a^(m+n) (WRONG).
   - sqrt(a + b) = sqrt(a) + sqrt(b) (WRONG).
assuming sqrt(x^2 + y^2) = x + y.

mistakes.source: F1.6: SPECIAL PRODUCTS AND FACTORIZATION IDENTITIES
mistakes.text:
forgetting the middle term; sign errors in a^3 + b^3
   (the second factor is a^2 - ab + b^2, with MINUS ab).
   a^2 + b^2 does NOT factorize over the reals.

forgetting that b^k carries its own coefficient (e.g. 2^k
   above); sign alternation for (a-b)^n.

mistakes.source: F1.8: QUADRATIC FORMULA AND COMPLETING THE SQUARE
mistakes.text:
sign of -b when b is negative (-(-5) = +5); dividing only
   part of the numerator by 2a; losing the factor 4 in 4ac.

Canceling a factor and forgetting the removed
point: f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) equals x + 1 only for x != 1. Its
domain excludes 1 (the graph has a "hole").

reading (f o g) as "f times g" or applying them in the
   wrong order.
f^(-1)(x) = 1/f(x) (WRONG). Forgetting domain restrictions.
x^2 (power) vs 2^x (exponential): derivative rules differ.

- log(x + y) = log x + log y (WRONG).  - (log x)^2 vs log(x^2).
   - log x / log y = log(x - y) (WRONG; it is a change of base only).
   - Forgetting to check the domain after solving log equations.

treating e as a variable; e^x vs x^e; thinking ln means
   log base 10.

letting delta depend on x; delta may depend only on epsilon
   (and a).

splitting a limit when one piece does not exist, e.g.
   lim (sin(1/x) * x) cannot be handled by splitting
   lim sin(1/x) (does not exist). (Squeeze theorem needed; F2.5.)

bounds that do not converge to the same L; using the
   theorem when the inequality holds only at isolated points.

using degrees; forgetting the constant when the
   argument is not x (sin(3x)/x tends to 3, not 1).

applying the quotient rule to f/g inside L'Hopital's rule.
   Using it when the form is not 0/0 or inf/inf, e.g.
   lim[x -> 0] (x+1)/(x+2) = 1/2 (just substitute).

assuming "limit exists" implies "continuous"; the limit
   might not equal f(a). Assuming the converse: continuity does NOT
   imply differentiability (|x| at 0, Module 3).

mistakes.source: F2.7: INTERMEDIATE VALUE THEOREM (IVT) AND EXTREME VALUE THEOREM
mistakes.text:
applying IVT to a discontinuous function (1/x on
   [-1, 1] changes sign but has no root) or EVT to an open interval.

- Forgetting to cancel h before taking the limit (gives 0/0).
   - Using (f(x+h))^2 instead of f(x+h) squared correctly; expand
     carefully.
   - Treating dy/dx as a literal fraction in contexts where it is not
     (but chain rule "canceling" works as a mnemonic).
   - Confusing f'(a) (number) with f'(x) (function).
   - Believing continuous implies differentiable.

mistakes.source: F3.2: TANGENT LINE AND LINEAR APPROXIMATION
mistakes.text: using a linear approximation far from a.

mistakes.source: F3.3: CONSTANT, CONSTANT-MULTIPLE AND SUM RULES
mistakes.text:
the product and quotient are NOT term-by-term: (fg)' !=
   f'g'.

bringing the exponent down but forgetting to subtract 1;
   differentiating 1/x^3 as 1/(3x^2); using the power rule on 2^x.
(fg)' = f'g'. Forgetting one of the two terms.

swapping the order in the numerator; forgetting to square
   the denominator; differentiating top and bottom separately.

forgetting the inner derivative; evaluating f' at x instead
   of g(x); stopping after one layer of a nested function.

mistakes.source: F3.8: DERIVATIVE TABLE (memorize; each derived from the rules)

mistakes.text: using the power rule (x^x)' = x * x^(x-1).

forgetting y' when differentiating a y term; dividing by
   zero at points of vertical tangent.

mistakes.source: F3.11: MONOTONICITY TEST (FIRST-DERIVATIVE TEST FOR INCREASE/DECREASE)
mistakes.text:
requiring f' > 0 everywhere for 'increasing'
   (isolated zeros are fine); testing the sign at one point instead of
   on the whole interval.

mistakes.source: F3.12: CRITICAL POINTS AND THE FIRST-DERIVATIVE TEST
mistakes.text:
assuming f'(c) = 0 means an extremum; forgetting
   points where f' does not exist; ignoring endpoints.

mistakes.source: F3.13: CLOSED-INTERVAL METHOD (for global extrema on [a, b])
mistakes.text:
forgetting endpoints; not checking that the critical point
   is inside the interval.

mistakes.source: F3.14: SECOND DERIVATIVE, CONCAVITY, SECOND-DERIVATIVE TEST
mistakes.text:
"f''(c) = 0 means inflection point" (not necessarily, see
   x^4); mixing up "concave up" with "increasing".

forgetting + C; applying the power rule with n = -1
   (int x^(-1) dx = ln|x| + C, not x^0/0).

counting area below the axis as positive (the integral is
   signed; for total area use int |f|); swapping limits without a sign
   change.

forgetting to evaluate at BOTH limits; subtracting in the
   wrong order; using FTC over a discontinuity.

forgetting the constant factor (du = 2x dx but only x dx is
   present: introduce 1/2); not converting limits; leaving x in the
   integrand after substitution.

choosing u and dv the wrong way round (makes the integral
   harder); sign errors; forgetting the boundary term uv in definite
   integrals.

bottom minus top; ignoring crossings; using signed integral
   when asked for area.

applying FTC across the singularity; treating
   inf - inf as zero; assuming all integrals to infinity diverge (or
   converge).

using n instead of n - 1 in a_n = a_1 + (n - 1) d;
   applying the geometric sum with r = 1.

mistakes.source: F5.3: INFINITE SERIES, PARTIAL SUMS AND THE GEOMETRIC SERIES
mistakes.text:
using the formula when |r| >= 1; using the wrong first term
   when the sum starts at k = 1 instead of 0 (the first term is a r, not
   a).

forgetting endpoint checks; writing R from the ratio test
   as the answer for the interval; mixing the ratio of terms with the
   ratio of coefficients.

differentiating at the boundary of the interval; claiming
   the interval of convergence stays the same (endpoints can change).

mistakes.source: F6.1: VECTOR ADDITION AND SCALAR MULTIPLICATION
mistakes.text:
adding vectors of different lengths; in Python, list
   + list concatenates while array + array adds.

confusing the dot product (scalar) with the cross product
   (vector, 3D only) or with element-wise multiplication (a vector;
   Python u * v on NumPy arrays is element-wise!). Using it on vectors
   of different lengths.

forgetting the square root; mixing L1/L2 in regularization
   (Lasso = L1, Ridge = L2).

confusing it with the dot product (a vector versus a
   scalar); applying it in dimensions other than 3.

mistakes.source: F6.5: MATRIX ADDITION AND SCALAR MULTIPLICATION
mistakes.text:
adding matrices of different shapes (NumPy may
   broadcast silently: check shapes); confusing it with matrix
   multiplication.

multiplying element-wise (Hadamard) by mistake; assuming
   commutativity; wrong dimension bookkeeping; applying (AB)^T = A^T B^T
   (WRONG order).

(AB)^T = A^T B^T (wrong order); forgetting that v^T
   w is a scalar but v w^T is a matrix.

inverting a non-square or singular matrix; (AB)^(-1) =
   A^(-1) B^(-1) (WRONG order); thinking A^(-1) means 1/A element-wise.

det(A + B) = det A + det B (WRONG); det(cA) = c det A
   (WRONG); sign errors in cofactor expansion; forgetting that a
   determinant close to 0 can be a scaling issue, not true singularity.

mistakes.source: F7.1: ELEMENTARY ROW OPERATIONS AND GAUSSIAN ELIMINATION
F7.2: CLASSIFICATION OF SOLUTIONS (ROUCHE-CAPELLI / RANK CRITERION)
mistakes.text:
judging rank from the coefficient matrix only
   (compare with the augmented matrix); concluding 'unique solution'
   just because m = n without checking pivots.

mistakes.source: F7.3: HOMOGENEOUS SYSTEM AND THE STRUCTURE OF SOLUTIONS
mistakes.text:
forgetting that a homogeneous system always has the
   trivial solution; declaring "no solution".

forgetting that closure under both operations must
   hold; thinking vectors must be arrows or lists of numbers.

checking closure but forgetting that the zero vector must be
   included (a shifted line is closed under nothing useful).

thinking two vectors always span a plane (not if one is a
   multiple of the other); thinking the span is just the finite list.

"pairwise non-parallel implies independent" (false for 3 or
   more vectors, e.g. the three vectors above); checking the rows instead
   of the columns when the vectors are written as columns (for a
   square matrix row rank = column rank, so it is fine there).

calling any spanning set a basis (must also be independent);
   assuming the standard basis is the only one.

mistakes.source: F8.6: THE FOUR FUNDAMENTAL SUBSPACES OF A (m x n)
mistakes.text:
taking pivot columns from the RREF instead of from A;
   mixing up which space lives in R^m vs R^n.
using the number of ROWS instead of columns in the formula.

allowing v = 0; assuming every matrix has real
   eigenvalues; forgetting that any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector
   is also an eigenvector.

forgetting v != 0; computing det(A) - lambda instead of
   det(A - lambda I); sign errors; reporting only the eigenvalue and
   not the eigenvector; thinking eigenvalues of A + B = eigenvalues of A
   + eigenvalues of B (false).

assuming eigenvectors of non-symmetric matrices are
   orthogonal.

mistakes.source: F9.5: POSITIVE DEFINITE AND SEMI-DEFINITE MATRICES
mistakes.text:
testing PD only via diagonal entries (positive diagonal is
   necessary, not sufficient); applying the tests to non-symmetric
   matrices; confusing PD with "all entries positive".

mistakes.source: F10.1: INNER PRODUCT AND INDUCED NORM
mistakes.text:
forgetting the positivity axiom (e.g. the Lorentzian
   "inner product" in relativity is not one); mixing inner and outer
   products (u v^T is a matrix).

using the formula with dependent columns (A^T A
   singular); forgetting that P is symmetric and idempotent (P^2 = P).

forgetting to normalize; subtracting projections onto the
   original a_i instead of the new q_i; applying it to dependent vectors.

mistakes.source: F10.5: LEAST-SQUARES SOLUTION AND NORMAL EQUATIONS
mistakes.text:
inverting A^T A explicitly on ill-conditioned data (use QR or
   SVD); forgetting the intercept column of ones; interpreting a
   least-squares fit as causal; treating least squares as "exact".

confusing singular values with eigenvalues (they coincide
   only for symmetric PSD matrices); treating sign differences between
   software outputs as errors; forgetting that SVD of the CENTERED data
   matrix is what gives PCA.

inverting a zero singular value (blows up noise);
   forming A^T A (squares the condition number).

dividing by n in one library and n - 1 in another;
   computing it from uncentered data.

not centering; not standardizing features with different
   scales (the largest-variance unit dominates); fitting PCA on the
   test set (data leakage, Module 46); interpreting a PC sign as
   meaningful; assuming high variance means high predictive power.

forgetting the absolute value; mis-reading the sign of c;
   using m1 m2 = 1 for perpendicular (it is -1).

mistakes.source: F11.3: LINES IN 3D (PARAMETRIC AND VECTOR FORM)
mistakes.text: assuming that lines in 3D that do not meet must be parallel.
forgetting to add the completed-square terms to BOTH sides.

confusing the one-sheet and two-sheet hyperboloids
   (sign pattern); forgetting that a missing variable gives a cylinder.

mistakes.source: F12.2: HIGHER-ORDER PARTIAL DERIVATIVES AND CLAIRAUT'S THEOREM
mistakes.text:
mixing up the order convention; assuming symmetry
   without continuity.

treating the gradient as a scalar; computing it at the wrong
   point; confusing "gradient" (vector of partials of a scalar function)
   with the Jacobian (matrix of partials of a vector function).
forgetting to normalize the direction vector.
forgetting a path; confusing partial and total derivatives.

mistakes.source: F12.6: CRITICAL POINTS AND THE HESSIAN MATRIX
F12.7: TANGENT PLANE AND LINEARIZATION  [multivariable version of F3.2]
mistakes.text:
using it far from (a, b); forgetting that it is the
   first-order Taylor polynomial.

forgetting to impose g = 0 together with the
   gradient equations; not checking whether a candidate is a maximum or
   a minimum.

mistakes.source: F13.1: DOUBLE INTEGRAL AND ITERATED INTEGRALS
F13.2: COORDINATE SYSTEMS AND AREA/VOLUME ELEMENTS
mistakes.text:
forgetting the Jacobian factor r or rho^2 sin(phi); mixing the
   roles of theta and phi; wrong limits (phi up to pi, not 2 pi).

forgetting the absolute value; using J of the inverse map
   inverted (use the right direction); not checking one-to-one.

mistakes.source: F14.1: SLOPE OF A PARAMETRIC CURVE
mistakes.text:
differentiating dy/dx with respect to x as if it were t:
   the second derivative needs the extra division by dx/dt.

mistakes.source: F14.2: VECTOR-VALUED FUNCTIONS OF ONE VARIABLE
mistakes.text:
confusing speed (a scalar |v|) and velocity (a vector);
   assuming zero acceleration at constant speed (direction changes).

forgetting the square root; integrating a velocity vector
   instead of its magnitude; including a repeated traversal.

mistakes.source: F14.4: DISTANCE FROM A POINT ON A CURVE TO THE ORIGIN
mistakes.text:
minimizing the distance when the squared distance is easier.
   (Both are fine as long as you minimize the right quantity.)

confusing ODEs with PDEs; forgetting the arbitrary
   constants of the general solution; not checking a solution by
   substitution.

assuming a solution exists for all t because the right-hand
   side looks harmless.

not dividing by the coefficient of y' first (reading P from
   x y' + 2y as 2); forgetting to multiply the RIGHT side by mu; leaving
   out the 1/mu when solving for y; forgetting C.

using years for k and months for t; using the half-life as k;
   forgetting that cooling approaches T_env, not zero.

mistakes.source: F16.4: EQUILIBRIA OF AUTONOMOUS EQUATIONS y' = f(y)
mistakes.text:
confusing stable/unstable; forgetting equilibrium solutions
   when separating variables; assuming every solution converges.

using too large a step; confusing local (per step)
   and global (accumulated) error.

- Treating Big-O as exact running time or as "worst case" (they are
     different ideas: worst-case is about INPUTS; O is about FUNCTIONS).
   - Saying O(2n) differs from O(n); writing O(n + log n) instead of O(n).
   - Forgetting that hidden costs exist (string concatenation in a loop;
     "x in list" is O(n)).
   - Using the same n for unrelated inputs.

mistakes.source: F18.1: SIMPLE HASH FUNCTION AND LOAD FACTOR
mistakes.text:
using mutable objects (lists) as keys (unhashable in
   Python); assuming ordering (hash tables are unordered conceptually;
   Python dicts preserve insertion order as an implementation guarantee,
   not sorted order); poor hash functions (e.g. k mod 10 with keys that
   are all multiples of 10); forgetting that lookup needs equality
   comparison after hashing.

mistakes.source: F20.1: LOWER BOUND FOR COMPARISON SORTING
mistakes.text:
claiming a comparison sort faster than n log n in
   the worst case; forgetting that the bound is about the worst case.

mistakes.source: F23.1: THE STANDARD LAWS  (hold for all Boolean A, B, C)
mistakes.text:
see the warning about the second distributive law;
   confusing identity (A ^ 1 = A) with null (A ^ 0 = 0).

forgetting to flip AND/OR; negating only one side; in pandas
   using and/or/not (error: ambiguous truth value of a Series) instead of
   &, |, ~ with BRACKETS around each comparison (& binds tighter than
   comparisons).

confusing selection (rows) with projection
   (columns); ignoring NULLs in joins.

mistakes.source: F25.1: JOIN ALGORITHMS AND THEIR COST (R with r rows, S with s rows)
mistakes.text:
joining on non-unique keys (row explosion); ignoring
   skewed key values.

summing floating-point partials in different orders gives
   slightly different results (floating-point addition is not exactly
   associative); numerical reproducibility is not exact.

mistakes.source: F26.2: GLOBAL MEAN FROM PARTITION MEANS
mistakes.text:
averaging averages; averaging percentages without weights;
   weighting by the wrong quantity (use the denominator of each rate).

using the formula with large means (cancellation);
   mixing n and n - 1.

mistakes.source: F26.4: COMBINING VARIANCES (STABLE, PARALLEL / CHAN ET AL. FORM)
mistakes.text:
using sample vs population denominators inconsistently across
   partitions (n_i - 1 vs n_i); sending only local variances and means
   (variance AND n_i are needed, plus the mean: with sample variances
   v_i, use M2_i = (n_i - 1) v_i); using the sum-of-squares formula on
   large, tightly clustered values.

thinking nondeterminism adds computing power to finite automata
   (it adds convenience, not power; it does for other machine types).

unescaped special characters; using regular
   expressions for nested structure.

mistakes.source: F27.5: PUMPING LEMMA FOR REGULAR LANGUAGES

mistakes.text:
forgetting that f is a fraction of the ORIGINAL time; assuming
   linear speed-up; ignoring overhead.

weights that do not match the quantity (e.g. weighting
   rates by something other than their denominators); dividing by
   the number of items rather than the sum of weights.

forgetting to sort; mis-handling even n; assuming the median of
   combined groups equals a combination of group medians (Module 26.5).

unequal widths without density scaling; unlabeled axes (counts
   vs density); extreme outliers stretching the x-axis; histogram of
   categorical data.

reading values of the ECDF as densities; forgetting the
   jump-size rule for ties.

calling a distribution symmetric because the mean equals the
   median (not sufficient); confusing the direction ("right skew" means
   the TAIL is on the right, the bulk on the left).

using the range for skewed data with outliers;
   comparing ranges across different sample sizes.

mixing quartile conventions when comparing across software;
   reporting range for skewed data with outliers.
OTHER ROBUST SPREAD: median absolute deviation MAD = median |x_i - median|
   (for 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: median 4.5, absolute deviations 2.5, 0.5, 0.5,
   0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 4.5 -> MAD = 0.5).

mistakes.source: F31.3: POPULATION VARIANCE AND STANDARD DEVIATION
mistakes.text:
using this formula on a sample (underestimates, see below);
   forgetting the square root for SD; confusing variance units.

mistakes.source: F31.4: SAMPLE VARIANCE AND SAMPLE STANDARD DEVIATION
mistakes.text:
dividing by n for a sample; dividing by n - 1 for a
   complete population; software defaults (NumPy np.var and np.std:
   ddof = 0; pandas .var/.std: ddof = 1; statistics.variance: n - 1,
   statistics.pvariance: n); computing the computational form with huge
   means (cancellation; Module 26); n = 1 (undefined).

reading magnitude as strength; dividing by n vs n - 1
   inconsistently (state the convention); concluding independence from
   zero covariance.

interpreting r as a percentage of association (r = 0.5 is not
   "50% related": r^2 = 0.25); interpreting r = 0 as independence;
   computing r on data with an outlier/leverage point without looking at
   the scatter plot; correlating ratios sharing a common denominator
   (spurious correlation); using it for categorical or strongly
   nonlinear relations.

mistakes.source: F32.3: INVARIANCE OF CORRELATION UNDER LINEAR TRANSFORMATIONS
mistakes.text:
expecting r to be unchanged by log transforms;
   forgetting that a negative scale factor flips the sign.

assuming outcomes are equally likely when they are not (e.g.
   "it either rains or it does not, so 50%"); unordered outcomes for
   multi-object experiments; probabilities that do not sum to 1.

computing "at least one" by adding single-event
   probabilities (double counts; see addition rule).

forgetting to subtract the overlap; using the disjoint form
   when events overlap (can give probability above 1: a warning sign).

multiplying probabilities of dependent events;
   confusing 'and' (multiply) with 'or' (add and subtract the overlap).

adding when stages should be multiplied (and vice versa);
   forgetting restrictions (no repeats).

using this when order does not matter; forgetting the division
   for identical items.

using permutations when the problem says "group", "committee",
   "hand", "subset"; double counting by treating a combination as ordered.

mistakes.source: F33.8: PROBABILITY FOR SAMPLING WITHOUT REPLACEMENT (HYPERGEOMETRIC)
mistakes.text:
using independent-trial (binomial) formulas for small
   populations; forgetting that denominators shrink (N, N-1, N-2, ...).

the "confusion of the inverse" (treating P(A | B) as
   P(B | A)): "most terrorists are X" is not "most X are terrorists";
   conditioning on the wrong event; forgetting to restrict the sample
   space; dividing by P(A) instead of P(B).

(very frequent)
   - Confusing MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with INDEPENDENT. If A and B are mutually
     exclusive and both have positive probability they are DEPENDENT
     (if A occurs, B cannot: P(B | A) = 0 != P(B)).
   - The gambler's fallacy: after 5 heads in a row the next toss is still
     50% heads (independent tosses).
   - Assuming independence for convenience (multiplying probabilities of
     correlated events understates joint risk).

using unconditional probabilities for the later factors when
   events are dependent.

weights that do not sum to 1; overlapping cases; using
   P(B_i | A) instead of P(A | B_i).

ignoring the prior (BASE RATE FALLACY); equating
   P(A | B) with P(B | A) (PROSECUTOR'S FALLACY: P(evidence | innocent)
   small does not mean P(innocent | evidence) small); not summing over
   ALL alternative explanations in the denominator.

mistakes.source: F34.6: PREDICTIVE VALUES FROM SENSITIVITY, SPECIFICITY AND PREVALENCE
mistakes.text: treating sensitivity as PPV; ignoring prevalence.

confusing the random variable X with an observed
   value x (a fixed number); treating category labels as numbers without
   justification.

PMF values not summing to 1; using a PMF for a continuous
   variable.

treating f(x) as a probability (it may exceed 1); forgetting
   to check normalization; integrating over the wrong limits; confusing
   f with the CDF F.

forgetting that F accumulates from the left; using P(a < X < b)
   = F(b) - F(a) for discrete variables without care about endpoints
   (P(a < X <= b) is the exact version); confusing the CDF with the PDF.

mistakes.source: F35.5: CONTINUOUS UNIFORM DISTRIBUTION U(a, b)
mistakes.text:
forgetting the density is zero outside [a, b]; using the
   continuous variance formula for the discrete uniform.

using p as a percentage (0 to 100) instead of a
   number in [0, 1]; forgetting that the variance is largest at p = 0.5.

using the binomial when trials are dependent; forgetting the
   binomial coefficient; confusing P(X = k) with P(X <= k); using the
   normal approximation for small n p or extreme p.

mixing rate and scale; using it for lifetimes with wear-out
   (not memoryless); forgetting x >= 0.

mistakes.source: F36.1: EXPECTED VALUE (MEAN) OF A RANDOM VARIABLE

mistakes.text:
thinking independence is needed for the sum rule; extending the
   rule to variances (it needs independence/covariance); applying to
   non-linear functions.

mistakes.source: F36.4: MOMENTS AND THE MOMENT GENERATING FUNCTION
mistakes.text:
mixing raw and central moments; forgetting to divide by
   sigma^k for standardized moments; assuming all moments exist.

E[g(X)] = g(E[X]); forgetting the Jacobian factor; applying the
   monotone formula to non-monotone g; forgetting that standardization
   changes the scale of the units.

ignoring endpoint inclusion for discrete variables ("at least 3"
   vs "more than 3").

mistakes.source: F37.1: SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION OF A STATISTIC
mistakes.text:
confusing the sampling distribution of x_bar with
   the distribution of the data; thinking only one sample exists.

mistakes.source: F37.2: MEAN AND VARIANCE OF THE SAMPLE MEAN
mistakes.text:
forgetting independence; confusing sigma/sqrt(n)
   with sigma; using it for dependent data.

the gambler's fallacy (past deviations are not
   'corrected'); applying it to distributions without a finite mean
   (Cauchy).

"with n > 30 the data are normal"; applying it to
   heavy-tailed data without checking; ignoring dependence.

calling an estimate (a number) biased (bias belongs to the
   estimator); assuming unbiased means accurate; thinking all
   "natural" estimators are unbiased; forgetting that s is not unbiased
   even though s^2 is.

mistakes.source: F37.6: VARIANCE OF AN ESTIMATOR, EFFICIENCY AND MSE
mistakes.text:
ignoring variance; thinking low bias alone justifies an
   estimator; confusing the variance of the estimator with the variance of
   the data.
equating consistency with unbiasedness.

confusing standard DEVIATION (spread of the data) with
   standard ERROR (spread of the estimate); reporting SD when SE is
   meant; assuming the SE shrinks with more data that is biased or
   dependent; using SE of a mean to describe individual variation.

using the wrong number of equations; using central/raw moments
   inconsistently; forgetting that the second moment includes mu^2.

treating L(theta) as a probability of theta;
   multiplying densities of dependent observations.

maximizing L(theta) when the support depends on theta
   without checking boundaries; forgetting to verify a maximum; confusing the
   MLE of sigma^2 (divide by n) with s^2; treating the likelihood as a
   probability of the parameter; using non-independent data in a product
   likelihood; reporting a local maximum.

mistakes.source: F38.4: FISHER INFORMATION AND THE CRAMER-RAO BOUND
mistakes.text:
expecting the MLE to be unbiased; applying asymptotic results
   with tiny n; ignoring that the bound applies to UNBIASED estimators
   only.

reading individual coefficients of a non-identified model;
   assuming optimization failure when the likelihood is genuinely flat.

choosing alpha after seeing the p-value; reading alpha as the
   probability that H0 is true; treating 0.05 as a magic boundary.

mistakes.source: F39.2: GENERAL FORM OF A TEST STATISTIC
mistakes.text:
using the sd instead of the SE in the denominator;
   using the wrong null distribution.

mistakes.source: F39.3: z-TEST FOR A MEAN (sigma known, or large n)
mistakes.text:
using z when sigma is estimated from a small sample
   (use t); confusing one-sided and two-sided p-values.

using n instead of n - 1 for the degrees of freedom;
   using z critical values with small samples.

calling "not significant" a proof of no effect in a low-power
   study; confusing alpha with beta or with power; computing "post-hoc
   power" from the observed p-value (uninformative).

mistakes.source: F39.7: CONFIDENCE INTERVAL FOR A MEAN
mistakes.text:
reading 95% as the proportion of DATA inside the interval (that
   is a prediction interval, much wider); comparing two CIs for overlap as
   a substitute for testing the difference (overlap is not a reliable test);
   using z instead of t for small n; applying Wald proportions to tiny
   counts.

using an independent test on paired data (or vice
   versa); using the pooled test with very unequal variances and unequal
   sample sizes; dropping the sign when interpreting direction; deciding
   the test after seeing the results; running t-tests on many features
   without correction.

mistakes.source: F40.1: THE SIMPLE LINEAR REGRESSION MODEL
mistakes.text:
treating the error eps and the residual e as the
   same thing; forgetting that the model is about the conditional mean.

mistakes.source: F40.2: LEAST SQUARES ESTIMATES FOR SIMPLE REGRESSION
mistakes.text:
interpreting the slope as causal; extrapolating beyond
   the data (see 40.2); interpreting the intercept literally; mixing up y
   on x with x on y (the two regression lines are different unless r = +/-
   1: b_1(y on x) = r s_y/s_x but b_1(x on y) = r s_x/s_y); reversing the
   order of x and y in S_xy/S_xx.

mistakes.source: F40.3: GOODNESS OF FIT: SST, SSR, SSE AND R^2
mistakes.text:
"high R^2 means a correct/causal model" (no); "low R^2 means
   the model is useless" (in noisy social data R^2 = 0.1 can still be
   informative; the slope may be well determined); comparing R^2 across
   different response transformations; using training R^2 as evidence of
   predictive performance (use held-out data, Module 46); forgetting that
   R^2 can be negative on test data.

mistakes.source: F40.4: INFERENCE FOR THE SLOPE AND INTERCEPT
mistakes.text:
reading a small p-value for the slope as a large effect or good
   prediction; confusing the p-value of the slope with the overall
   goodness of fit; ignoring the CI.

mistakes.source: F40.5: PREDICTION: MEAN RESPONSE vs NEW OBSERVATION
mistakes.text:
using the CI for the mean when a prediction for one case is
   needed; extrapolating; reporting the prediction without uncertainty.
   (Note: the standard prediction interval assumes normal, constant-
   variance errors.)

interpreting a coefficient without "other variables held
   fixed"; comparing raw coefficients of variables on different scales
   (use standardized coefficients); including all dummies for a
   categorical variable plus an intercept (dummy-variable trap): use k - 1
   dummies, the omitted group is the REFERENCE category; adding variables
   until R^2 is high (overfitting); ignoring that t-tests of individual
   coefficients depend on which other variables are included.

confusing "outlier" (large residual) with "high leverage" (extreme
   x); removing influential points silently; assuming a point with a tiny
   residual is harmless.

mistakes.source: F40.8: MULTICOLLINEARITY AND THE VARIANCE INFLATION FACTOR
mistakes.text:
removing variables solely because their t-values are low when
   they are collinear (drop one at a time, using domain knowledge);
   thinking multicollinearity biases OLS (it does not bias, it inflates
   variance); the dummy-variable trap (perfect collinearity).

"controlling for everything": do NOT adjust for MEDIATORS (on the
   path X -> M -> Y; removes part of the true effect) or COLLIDERS (a
   variable caused by both X and Y; conditioning creates spurious
   association); thinking R^2 or significance shows confounding is absent.

computing the scaler on the whole dataset before splitting
   (leakage); scaling dummy variables unnecessarily; forgetting to apply
   the saved transformation at prediction time; using min-max with
   unbounded outliers.

assuming that a successful training run found the global
   optimum of a non-convex objective.

learning rate too large; not scaling features (huge
   condition number); stopping criterion too loose or tight; computing
   gradients incorrectly (verify with finite differences, "gradient
   checking"); expecting the global minimum for non-convex losses;
   forgetting to shuffle data in SGD.

mistakes.source: F43.3: NEWTON-RAPHSON FOR ROOT FINDING (ONE VARIABLE)
mistakes.text:
starting near a point with f' = 0; expecting
   convergence from any start.

inverting H explicitly; applying Newton where H is not
   positive definite (a maximum or saddle attracts it); divide-by-zero
   when f'' = 0; using it for huge parameter counts (neural nets).

using it for hundreds of parameters; trusting convergence
   without restarts; poor initial simplex scale; applying it where
   gradients are cheap (use gradient methods).

reading leaf proportions as true probabilities when leaves are
   tiny; forgetting that regression trees cannot extrapolate beyond the
   range of leaf means (the prediction never exceeds the training y-range).
forgetting the "1 -"; using counts instead of proportions.

using log base 10 inconsistently; forgetting that log2 of a
   fraction is negative (hence the leading minus); computing 0 * log 0
   as NaN.

unweighted averaging of child impurities; thinking
   Gini and entropy give very different trees (they usually agree);
   computing gain relative to the wrong parent; considering thresholds
   at data values instead of midpoints (equivalent in effect but check
   the convention).

mistakes.source: F44.5: SPLITTING CRITERION FOR REGRESSION TREES
mistakes.text: expecting a smooth fit (steps only); extrapolation.

choosing the tree size by training error (always favours the full
   tree); tuning ccp_alpha on the test set; ignoring that a pruned tree can
   still be unstable.

forgetting that bootstrap samples contain duplicates; thinking
   the bootstrap sample is smaller than n (it has n draws but only about
   0.632 n distinct cases).

expecting bagging to reduce bias; using too few
   bootstrap models.

mistakes.source: F45.3: VARIANCE OF AN AVERAGE OF CORRELATED PREDICTORS

mistakes.text:
using forest training accuracy as performance; using OOB after
   tuning hyperparameters on it and reporting it as final; too few trees.

mistakes.source: F46.1: BIAS-VARIANCE DECOMPOSITION OF EXPECTED TEST ERROR
mistakes.text:
forgetting the irreducible term; thinking low training error
   means low bias AND low variance; trying to get test MSE below sigma^2.

fitting scalers/imputers/feature selectors on the whole
   dataset before CV (leakage); using the CV score of the BEST configuration
   as a performance estimate (selection bias, Module 47); forgetting to
   shuffle sorted data (see below); reporting the SE as SD/sqrt(k) as if
   folds were independent; using random k-fold on time series or grouped
   data.

mistakes.source: F46.3: CONFUSION MATRIX AND DERIVED CLASSIFICATION METRICS
mistakes.text:
using accuracy on imbalanced data; averaging F1 across classes
   without stating the average (macro/micro/weighted); comparing precision
   across datasets with different prevalence; computing metrics on training
   data.

mistakes.source: F46.4: THRESHOLDS, ROC CURVE AND AUC
mistakes.text:
choosing the threshold 0.5 by default (tune it to the cost and
   prevalence, on validation data); reporting AUC when calibrated
   probabilities are needed (AUC ignores calibration).

feeding class labels instead of probabilities;
   ignoring calibration.

comparing RMSE across different target scales; using R^2 on
   training data; MSE dominated by outliers (use MAE/Huber when needed).

huge grids with many irrelevant dimensions; linear (rather than
   log) spacing for scale parameters; searching on the test set; grid
   boundary optimum.

using uniform instead of log-uniform sampling for scale
   parameters; too few iterations; ignoring the seed (not reproducible).
OTHER STRATEGIES [SUPPLEMENTARY]: SUCCESSIVE HALVING/HYPERBAND (give many
   configurations a small budget, keep the best half, repeat); BAYESIAN
   OPTIMIZATION (a surrogate model, e.g. Gaussian process or TPE, proposes
   promising configurations: Optuna, scikit-optimize); evolutionary search;
   manual search guided by learning curves. Nelder-Mead (Module 43) and
   gradient-based hyper-gradients are rarely used for noisy objectives.

reporting best_score_ of GridSearchCV as the expected test
   accuracy; running preprocessing outside the pipeline; reusing the same
   splits so that selection and evaluation are not independent; using the
   test set to select among models and then reporting it.
   (In a milder verified SVM example with 30 configurations and 80 cases,
   averaged over 10 datasets: best inner CV 0.679, nested 0.646, true
   accuracy of the tuned model 0.667: optimism of about 0.01 but a noisy
   estimator: nested CV on tiny data has a large variance, SD of single
   runs several points; the effect of selection bias grows with the
   number of configurations compared and shrinks with data size.)
OTHER WAYS TO AVOID OPTIMISM: three-way split (final test used ONCE);
   limit the number of candidates; pre-register the analysis; use the
   one-standard-error rule; keep an external validation set from a
   different time or site; treat the test score as a one-shot estimate.

mistakes.source: F48.1: LINEAR CLASSIFIER AND ITS DECISION BOUNDARY
mistakes.text:
treating logistic regression's boundary as curved (it is
   linear in the features given); reading coefficients on unscaled
   features as importance; forgetting the intercept; interpreting
   probabilities of an uncalibrated score.

using LDA with strongly non-normal features or unequal
   covariances without checking; p > n without shrinkage (singular
   Sigma); ignoring priors under imbalance; confusing LDA with Latent
   Dirichlet Allocation (topic model).

interpreting main effects alone when an interaction
   is present; omitting the main effects.

mistakes.source: F48.5: KERNEL FUNCTIONS AND THE KERNEL TRICK
mistakes.text:
not scaling features (distances dominated by the largest
   scale); gamma too large; assuming a kernel is always better than a
   linear model (with p >> n a linear kernel is usually enough); using
   an invalid (non-PSD) similarity as a kernel.

thinking all training points matter (only support vectors);
   assuming data are separable.

mistakes.source: F48.7: SOFT-MARGIN SVM, THE PARAMETER C AND REGULARIZATION
mistakes.text:
unscaled features; confusing C (penalty on errors: large
   C = weak regularization) with lambda (large lambda = strong
   regularization): C and lambda are inverses; scikit-learn's C for
   LogisticRegression/SVC is the INVERSE of regularization strength;
   tuning on the test set; using accuracy on imbalanced data (use
   class_weight and suitable metrics).

conditions.title: ABSOLUTE VALUE (definition)
conditions.text:
Defined for all real numbers. Beware: sqrt(x^2) = |x|, NOT x.
   (e.g. sqrt((-3)^2) = sqrt(9) = 3 = |-3|.)

conditions.title: ABSOLUTE-VALUE INEQUALITY RULES
conditions.text:
a > 0. If a < 0: |x| < a has NO solution (a distance
   cannot be negative); |x| > a is true for ALL x. If a = 0, |x| < 0 has
   no solution, |x| <= 0 has only x = 0.

conditions.title: TRIANGLE INEQUALITY
conditions.text: all real a, b.

conditions.title: EXPONENT (INDEX) LAWS
ROOTS AND RATIONALIZING
conditions.text:
sqrt(ab) = sqrt(a) sqrt(b) requires a, b >= 0.
   sqrt((-4)(-9)) = sqrt(36) = 6, but sqrt(-4) sqrt(-9) is not defined
   in the reals.

conditions.title: SPECIAL PRODUCTS AND FACTORIZATION IDENTITIES
conditions.text:
the identities hold for all real numbers and for any
   algebraic expressions in place of a and b; a^2 + b^2 has no real
   factorization; a^n + b^n factors over the reals only for odd n: a^n +
   b^n = (a + b)(a^(n-1) - a^(n-2) b + ... + b^(n-1)).

conditions.title: BINOMIAL THEOREM
conditions.text:
integer n >= 0 for a finite expansion. For non-integer n
   there is an infinite series version valid for |x| < 1 (Module 5).

conditions.title: QUADRATIC FORMULA AND COMPLETING THE SQUARE
conditions.text: a != 0. If a = 0 the equation is linear.

conditions.title: COMPOSITION OF FUNCTIONS
conditions.text:
g(x) must lie in the domain of f. Order matters:
   f o g is generally different from g o f.

conditions.title: INVERSE FUNCTION
conditions.text:
f must be one-to-one on the domain considered. If not,
   restrict the domain (sqrt is the inverse of x^2 on [0, inf)).

conditions.title: EXPONENTIAL FUNCTION
conditions.text:
b > 0 (so that b^x is defined for all real x).
   Domain R, range (0, inf), always positive, one-to-one.
   b^(x+y) = b^x b^y; b^(-x) = 1/b^x.

conditions.title: LOGARITHM
conditions.text:
x > 0 only. Logs of 0 or negative numbers are undefined
   (real logs). Domain (0, inf), range R.
   Laws do NOT apply to log(x + y) (no rule!).

conditions.title: EULER'S NUMBER e
conditions.text: the limit exists and is finite.

conditions.title: NATURAL LOGARITHM PROPERTIES
conditions.text:
ln x needs x > 0; the approximations are accurate only
   for small |h| (error about h^2/2); for |h| above about 0.3 use the
   exact values.

conditions.title: FORMAL (EPSILON-DELTA) DEFINITION  [Level 3 material]
conditions.text:
epsilon > 0 is arbitrary; delta may depend on epsilon and
   on the point a but not on x; f must be defined near a (except
   possibly at a).

conditions.title: BASIC LIMIT LAWS
conditions.text:
ALL the separate limits must exist. For a quotient the
   denominator's limit must be non-zero; if both limits are 0 you have
   an indeterminate form (2.5) and must do more work.

conditions.title: SQUEEZE THEOREM
conditions.text:
NOTE: g <= f <= h must hold on a neighbourhood of a (not
   everywhere necessarily).

conditions.title: IMPORTANT STANDARD LIMITS
conditions.text:
x tends to 0 (or infinity for the last limit); angles in
   radians.

conditions.title: L'HOPITAL'S RULE
conditions.text:
only for 0/0 or inf/inf. Applying it otherwise gives
   wrong answers. Other indeterminate forms must be converted first
   (0*inf -> f/(1/g); 1^inf, 0^0, inf^0 via logarithms).

conditions.title: CONTINUITY AT A POINT
conditions.text:
continuity on an interval means continuity at each of its
   points (one-sided at endpoints). Polynomials, exp, sin, cos are
   continuous on R; ln on (0, inf); rational functions are continuous
   wherever the denominator is non-zero; sums, products, compositions
   and quotients (denominator != 0) of continuous functions are
   continuous.

conditions.title: INTERMEDIATE VALUE THEOREM (IVT) AND EXTREME VALUE THEOREM
conditions.text:
Fails when f is not continuous or the interval is open/unbounded:
   f(x) = 1/x on (0,1] has no maximum.

conditions.title: DERIVATIVE (DEFINITION)
conditions.text:
- The limit must EXIST and be finite. If it does not, f is not
     differentiable at that point.
   - f must be defined near x (both sides).
   - Differentiable => continuous. CONVERSE FALSE: f(x) = |x| is
     continuous at 0 but not differentiable (left slope -1, right slope
     +1: a corner). Similarly a vertical tangent (cube root at 0) or a
     cusp gives no derivative. ReLU(x) = max(0,x) is not
     differentiable at 0; frameworks use a sub-gradient (conventionally
     0 or 1 at that point).

conditions.title: TANGENT LINE AND LINEAR APPROXIMATION
conditions.text:
f differentiable at a. Approximation is good only for
   small |x - a|; error is about (1/2) f''(a) (x-a)^2 (Taylor, Module 5).

conditions.title: CONSTANT, CONSTANT-MULTIPLE AND SUM RULES
conditions.text: f and g differentiable at x.

conditions.title: POWER RULE
conditions.text:
the variable is in the BASE and the exponent is a
   CONSTANT. For a CONSTANT base and variable exponent (2^x) the
   power rule does NOT apply (use F3.8). For x^x neither applies (use
   logarithmic differentiation, F3.9).

conditions.title: PRODUCT RULE
conditions.text: both differentiable. NOT (fg)' = f'g'.

conditions.title: QUOTIENT RULE
conditions.text: g(x) != 0. ORDER of the numerator matters (minus sign).

conditions.title: CHAIN RULE
conditions.text: g differentiable at x and f differentiable at g(x).

conditions.title: DERIVATIVE TABLE (memorize; each derived from the rules)
conditions.text:
ln x and 1/x need x > 0 (or x != 0); a^x needs a > 0;
   trigonometric derivatives assume radians; tan x needs cos x != 0.

conditions.title: LOGARITHMIC DIFFERENTIATION
conditions.text: f(x) > 0 (or use |f|).

conditions.title: IMPLICIT DIFFERENTIATION
conditions.text:
slope formula usually has y in the denominator; it fails
   (vertical tangent) where that denominator is 0.

conditions.title: MONOTONICITY TEST (FIRST-DERIVATIVE TEST FOR INCREASE/DECREASE)
conditions.text:
f continuous on I and differentiable inside. (The test
   gives a sufficient, not necessary, condition: f(x) = x^3 is
   increasing even though f'(0) = 0.)

conditions.title: CRITICAL POINTS AND THE FIRST-DERIVATIVE TEST
conditions.text: !! WARNING !! f'(c) = 0 does NOT guarantee an extremum.

conditions.title: CLOSED-INTERVAL METHOD (for global extrema on [a, b])
conditions.text:
continuity on a closed bounded interval guarantees
   existence (EVT, F2.7). On an open or unbounded domain extremes may not
   exist; study limits at the ends.

conditions.title: SECOND DERIVATIVE, CONCAVITY, SECOND-DERIVATIVE TEST
conditions.text:
f'' must exist near c; the test is inconclusive when
   f''(c) = 0 (x^4 has a minimum, x^3 none, -x^4 a maximum).

conditions.title: ANTIDERIVATIVE / INDEFINITE INTEGRAL
conditions.text:
f continuous on the interval guarantees an antiderivative
   exists. An antiderivative can exist yet have NO formula in elementary
   functions (e.g. e^(-x^2); this is why the normal CDF is a named
   special function, Module 35).

conditions.title: STANDARD INTEGRALS TABLE  (each is the derivative table reversed)
conditions.text:
the power formula needs n != -1; ln|x| is valid on any
   interval not containing 0 (C may differ on each side); a > 0 and a !=
   1 for a^x.

conditions.title: DEFINITE INTEGRAL (RIEMANN SUM DEFINITION)
FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF CALCULUS
conditions.text:
f continuous on [a, b]. In Part 2, the constant C cancels
   in F(b) - F(a), so no C is needed. If f has a discontinuity or an
   infinite spike inside [a,b], FTC must not be applied blindly
   (e.g. int[-1..1] 1/x^2 dx is NOT -2: the integrand blows up at 0).
g. the integral of marginal cost from 0 to 100 items is the total
   cost increase.

conditions.title: u-SUBSTITUTION
conditions.text:
g differentiable with continuous derivative; the
   integrand must contain g'(x) (up to a constant factor). In a
   definite integral, EITHER change the limits to u-values OR convert
   back to x before using the old limits; never mix them.

conditions.title: INTEGRATION BY PARTS
conditions.text:
f and g differentiable. Works best for a product of two
   different kinds of function. May need to be applied repeatedly or
   cyclically.

conditions.title: AREA BETWEEN TWO CURVES
conditions.text:
identify which curve is on top; take |...| / split when
   the order switches.

conditions.title: IMPROPER INTEGRAL
conditions.text:
break at interior singularities. Symmetric cancellation
   trick lim[t -> inf] int[-t..t] x dx = 0 does NOT make int[-inf..inf] x
   dx converge.
   P-TEST (standard benchmark):
     int[1..inf] 1/x^p dx converges iff p > 1, value 1/(p - 1).
     int[0..1]  1/x^p dx converges iff p < 1, value 1/(1 - p).
     int[0..inf] e^(-kx) dx = 1/k (k > 0).
   Comparison test: if 0 <= f <= g and int g converges then int f
   converges; if int f diverges then int g diverges.

conditions.title: CONVERGENCE OF A SEQUENCE
conditions.text:
limit must be a finite number. Otherwise the sequence
   DIVERGES (to infinity or by oscillation). Limit laws (F2.2) apply.
   Monotone Convergence Theorem: every bounded monotone (always
   non-decreasing, or always non-increasing) sequence converges.
   If a_n = f(n) and lim[x -> inf] f(x) = L then a_n -> L.

conditions.title: ARITHMETIC AND GEOMETRIC SEQUENCES
conditions.text:
the sum formula for the geometric case needs r != 1 (r =
   1 gives n a_1); the infinite sum needs |r| < 1 (F5.3).

conditions.title: INFINITE SERIES, PARTIAL SUMS AND THE GEOMETRIC SERIES
conditions.text:
the geometric series converges only for |r| < 1; the
   formula a/(1 - r) uses the FIRST term a, so the start index matters.

conditions.title: CONVERGENCE TESTS (a toolbox)
conditions.text:
comparison and integral tests need (eventually) positive
   terms; the ratio and root tests are inconclusive at rho = 1; the
   alternating series test needs decreasing terms tending to 0.

conditions.title: POWER SERIES
conditions.text: R = 0: only x = a; R = inf: all real x.

conditions.title: TAYLOR SERIES
conditions.text:
f infinitely differentiable at a; the series equals f only
   where the remainder -> 0 (inside the interval of convergence, for
   "analytic" functions). Not every infinitely differentiable function
   equals its Taylor series [Level 3: e^(-1/x^2)].

conditions.title: TERM-BY-TERM CALCULUS
conditions.text:
valid only inside |x - a| < R; at the endpoints
   convergence must be rechecked.

conditions.title: VECTOR ADDITION AND SCALAR MULTIPLICATION
conditions.text: only vectors of equal length can be added.

conditions.title: DOT (INNER) PRODUCT
conditions.text:
same length. Symmetric: u.v = v.u; bilinear;
   u.u = |u|^2 >= 0, and = 0 only for the zero vector.

conditions.title: NORM (LENGTH) OF A VECTOR
conditions.text:
v != 0 for a unit vector; every norm satisfies |v| >= 0
   (= 0 only for the zero vector), |c v| = |c||v|, and the triangle
   inequality.

conditions.title: CROSS PRODUCT [SUPPLEMENTARY; R^3 ONLY]
conditions.text:
defined only in R^3; anti-commutative (u x v = -(v x u));
   u x v = 0 exactly when u and v are parallel.

conditions.title: MATRIX ADDITION AND SCALAR MULTIPLICATION
conditions.text: Matrices must have identical dimensions.

conditions.title: MATRIX MULTIPLICATION
conditions.text:
- Inner dimensions must match: (m x n)(n x p). (2x3)(2x3) is
     undefined.
   - NOT commutative: AB != BA in general (the product may even exist
     for only one order).
   - Associative: (AB)C = A(BC). Distributive: A(B + C) = AB + AC.
   - (AB)^T = B^T A^T  (order reverses).
   - AB = 0 does NOT imply A = 0 or B = 0. AB = AC does NOT imply B = C.
   - Cost of multiplying two n x n matrices naively: O(n^3).

conditions.title: TRANSPOSE
conditions.text:
defined for every matrix; a symmetric matrix must be
   square; (AB)^T = B^T A^T reverses the order.

conditions.title: MATRIX INVERSE
conditions.text:
A must be SQUARE and non-singular (det != 0, equivalently
   rank n, linearly independent columns, Ax = 0 has only x = 0). A
   non-square matrix has no (two-sided) inverse.
   !! WARNING !! For numerical work, NEVER compute A^(-1) just to solve
   Ax = b; use elimination (np.linalg.solve). Inverting is slower and
   less accurate.

conditions.title: DETERMINANT
ELEMENTARY ROW OPERATIONS AND GAUSSIAN ELIMINATION
conditions.text:
DEFINITIONS
   ROW ECHELON FORM (REF):
     - any all-zero rows are at the bottom;
     - the leading entry (first nonzero entry, the PIVOT) of each nonzero
       row lies to the right of the pivot in the row above;
     - entries below each pivot are zero.
   REDUCED ROW ECHELON FORM (RREF): REF plus
     - every pivot equals 1;
     - each pivot is the only nonzero entry in its column.
   RREF of a matrix is UNIQUE; REF is not.
   Pivot columns = columns that contain pivots. Pivot variables
   (basic) correspond to pivot columns; FREE variables to non-pivot
   columns.

conditions.title: CLASSIFICATION OF SOLUTIONS (ROUCHE-CAPELLI / RANK CRITERION)
conditions.text:
& SHAPE EXPECTATIONS (for any field of numbers)
     m < n  (fewer equations than unknowns): never a unique solution
            (either none or infinitely many).
     m = n and det(A) != 0: exactly one solution for every b.
     m > n  (overdetermined): usually inconsistent; use LEAST SQUARES
            (Module 10).

conditions.title: HOMOGENEOUS SYSTEM AND THE STRUCTURE OF SOLUTIONS
conditions.text:
the structure x = x_p + x_h holds when Ax = b is
   consistent; x_h ranges over the whole null space of A.

conditions.title: VECTOR SPACE AXIOMS (summary)
conditions.text:
all axioms must hold; the set of vectors with positive
   entries is NOT a vector space (no 0, no negatives).

conditions.title: SUBSPACE TEST
conditions.text:
W must contain 0, and be closed under addition and scalar
   multiplication.

conditions.title: LINEAR COMBINATION AND SPAN
conditions.text:
TEST FOR MEMBERSHIP: b is in Span{v1, ..., vk} iff the system
   [v1 ... vk] c = b has a solution (Module 7).

conditions.title: LINEAR INDEPENDENCE
conditions.text:
TESTS
     (a) Form the matrix A with the vectors as COLUMNS. Independent iff
         Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution iff rank(A) = k (a pivot
         in every column).
     (b) k vectors in R^n with k = n: independent iff det(A) != 0.
     (c) More than n vectors in R^n are ALWAYS dependent.
     (d) Any set containing the zero vector is dependent. Two vectors are
         dependent iff one is a multiple of the other.

conditions.title: BASIS AND DIMENSION
conditions.text:
FACTS: dim(R^n) = n (standard basis e1 = (1,0,...,0), ..., en). In an
   n-dimensional space any n independent vectors form a basis; any set
   of more than n vectors is dependent; fewer than n cannot span.
   Polynomials of degree <= 2 form a 3-dimensional space with basis
   {1, x, x^2}. m x n matrices form an (mn)-dimensional space.

conditions.title: THE FOUR FUNDAMENTAL SUBSPACES OF A (m x n)
conditions.text:
HOW TO FIND BASES (using the RREF/REF of A)
     Column space: take the PIVOT COLUMNS of the ORIGINAL matrix A (not
        of the reduced matrix, since row operations change columns!).
     Row space: take the non-zero rows of the REF/RREF.
     Null space: solve Ax = 0, write the free variables as parameters;
        one basis vector per free variable ("special solutions").

conditions.title: RANK-NULLITY THEOREM
EIGENVALUE EQUATION
conditions.text:
only square matrices; v must be non-zero (the zero vector
   satisfies the equation trivially, which would be meaningless). If v is
   an eigenvector, so is every non-zero scalar multiple; eigenvectors are
   determined only up to scale, and the set of all eigenvectors for one
   lambda, plus 0, is a subspace (the EIGENSPACE).

conditions.title: CHARACTERISTIC EQUATION
conditions.text:
degree-n polynomial: n eigenvalues over the complex numbers
   (with multiplicity); real matrices may have complex eigenvalues
   (rotations). Triangular matrices: eigenvalues are the diagonal
   entries. Numerical computation uses iterative algorithms (QR
   algorithm), never the characteristic polynomial for large n.

conditions.title: DIAGONALIZATION
conditions.text:
A (n x n) is diagonalizable iff it has n linearly
   independent eigenvectors. Sufficient: n DISTINCT eigenvalues.
   Not diagonalizable: defective matrices (F9 section 9.3).

conditions.title: SPECTRAL THEOREM (REAL SYMMETRIC MATRICES)
conditions.text:
real symmetric (or complex Hermitian). Does NOT hold for
   general non-symmetric matrices.

conditions.title: POSITIVE DEFINITE AND SEMI-DEFINITE MATRICES
conditions.text:
the definition requires symmetry (non-symmetric matrices
   are handled by their symmetric part (A + A^T)/2).

conditions.title: INNER PRODUCT AND INDUCED NORM
conditions.text:
all three axioms must hold; equality in Cauchy-Schwarz
   iff the vectors are parallel (one a multiple of the other).

conditions.title: PROJECTION ONTO A SUBSPACE
conditions.text: columns of A MUST be independent.

conditions.title: GRAM-SCHMIDT
conditions.text:
inputs must be linearly independent (a zero v_j signals
   dependence). Classical Gram-Schmidt loses orthogonality numerically;
   Modified Gram-Schmidt or Householder reflections are preferred in
   software (np.linalg.qr uses Householder).

conditions.title: LEAST-SQUARES SOLUTION AND NORMAL EQUATIONS
conditions.text:
A^T A invertible iff the columns are independent. When
   columns are nearly dependent (multicollinearity), A^T A is
   ill-conditioned (condition number is SQUARED relative to A). Least
   squares is sensitive to outliers (squared errors). It is the maximum
   likelihood estimate under independent Gaussian noise of equal
   variance (Module 38/40).

conditions.title: SINGULAR VALUE DECOMPOSITION
conditions.text:
exists for every matrix (unlike eigendecomposition).
   Singular values are unique; singular vectors are unique only up to
   sign (and rotation within repeated singular values).

conditions.title: PSEUDO-INVERSE (MOORE-PENROSE) AND CONDITION NUMBER
conditions.text:
it exists for every matrix; for numerical rank decisions
   use a tolerance (singular values below about eps * sigma_max are
   treated as 0).

conditions.title: SAMPLE COVARIANCE MATRIX
conditions.text:
needs n >= 2; for the PD property need n - 1 >= p and no
   exact collinearity; the 1/(n-1) is the unbiased sample convention
   (1/n for population / MLE; state which one a library uses).

conditions.title: PRINCIPAL COMPONENT ANALYSIS
DISTANCE AND MIDPOINT FORMULAS
conditions.text:
Cartesian (perpendicular, equally-scaled) axes. If features
   have different units/scales, Euclidean distance on raw features is
   misleading (standardize first; Module 46).

conditions.title: EQUATIONS OF LINES (2D)
conditions.text:
vertical lines (x = k) have no slope; use the general
   form.

conditions.title: LINES IN 3D (PARAMETRIC AND VECTOR FORM)
conditions.text:
d != 0; the parametrization of a line is not unique (any
   point and any non-zero multiple of d work).

conditions.title: CIRCLE AND SPHERE
conditions.text:
If the right-hand side after completing the square is <= 0, there is no
   circle (a single point or empty set).

conditions.title: QUADRIC SURFACES (second-degree surfaces)
PARTIAL DERIVATIVE
conditions.text:
f must be defined near the point; existence of both
   partials at a point does NOT guarantee that f is continuous there
   (different from the single-variable case); differentiability needs
   continuous partials (sufficient).

conditions.title: HIGHER-ORDER PARTIAL DERIVATIVES AND CLAIRAUT'S THEOREM
conditions.text:
Clairaut needs f_xy and f_yx continuous near the point;
   counterexamples exist otherwise.

conditions.title: GRADIENT
conditions.text:
f differentiable at the point. grad f = 0 at a critical
   point.

conditions.title: DIRECTIONAL DERIVATIVE
conditions.text:
u must have length 1; if given a non-unit vector, divide
   by its length first.

conditions.title: MULTIVARIABLE CHAIN RULE
conditions.text: f differentiable (continuous partials suffice).

conditions.title: CRITICAL POINTS AND THE HESSIAN MATRIX
conditions.text:
continuous second partials. Critical points are only
   candidates; for GLOBAL extremes also examine the boundary and behavior
   at infinity. (On a closed bounded region: evaluate on the boundary as
   well; EVT, F2.7.)

conditions.title: TANGENT PLANE AND LINEARIZATION  [multivariable version of F3.2]
conditions.text:
f differentiable at (a, b); accurate only for small steps
   (error is second order, about (1/2) h^T H h).

conditions.title: CONSTRAINED OPTIMIZATION: LAGRANGE MULTIPLIERS [SUPPLEMENTARY]
conditions.text:
needs grad g != 0 at the optimum (regularity); it gives
   candidates, which must be checked as maxima or minima; inequality
   constraints need KKT (Appendix D).

conditions.title: DOUBLE INTEGRAL AND ITERATED INTEGRALS
conditions.text:
f continuous on R (Fubini: integrable and bounded suffices);
   the limits of the INNER integral may depend on the OUTER variable only,
   never on itself; the OUTER limits must be constants. You may swap the
   order if you also redraw the limits.

conditions.title: COORDINATE SYSTEMS AND AREA/VOLUME ELEMENTS
conditions.text: set the angular limits to cover the region exactly once.

conditions.title: CHANGE OF VARIABLES
conditions.text:
the map must be one-to-one (invertible) with continuous
   partial derivatives and J != 0.

conditions.title: SLOPE OF A PARAMETRIC CURVE
conditions.text:
dx/dt != 0 (dx/dt = 0 with dy/dt != 0 gives a vertical
   tangent); x(t) and y(t) differentiable.

conditions.title: VECTOR-VALUED FUNCTIONS OF ONE VARIABLE
conditions.text:
components differentiable; the unit tangent requires
   r'(t) != 0.

conditions.title: ARC LENGTH
conditions.text:
r' continuous; the curve should be traced ONCE over [a, b]
   (otherwise the formula gives total distance traveled, which
   counts repeats).

conditions.title: DISTANCE FROM A POINT ON A CURVE TO THE ORIGIN
conditions.text:
differentiable r(t); critical points of |r|^2 are where r
   is perpendicular to r' (2 r . r' = 0).

conditions.title: GENERAL FORM
PICARD-LINDELOF (EXISTENCE AND UNIQUENESS) THEOREM
conditions.text:
the guarantee is LOCAL (solutions may blow up in finite
   time) and sufficient, not necessary. When f_y fails to be continuous,
   uniqueness may fail.

conditions.title: SEPARATION OF VARIABLES
conditions.text:
dividing by h(y) is allowed only where h(y) != 0.
   Constants y* with h(y*) = 0 are EQUILIBRIUM solutions and must be
   checked separately (they may be lost by the division).

conditions.title: INTEGRATING FACTOR METHOD
conditions.text:
the equation must be LINEAR in y and put into STANDARD FORM
   (coefficient of y' equal to 1) before reading off P(x).

conditions.title: EXPONENTIAL GROWTH/DECAY MODEL
conditions.text:
k constant; resources unlimited for growth (otherwise
   logistic). Cooling law assumes uniform temperature of the object.

conditions.title: EQUILIBRIA OF AUTONOMOUS EQUATIONS y' = f(y)
conditions.text:
the equation is autonomous (no explicit t); linearization
   is conclusive when f'(y*) != 0.

conditions.title: EULER'S METHOD
conditions.text:
the global error is of order h (first-order accuracy);
   too large a step h can be unstable (for y' = -ky need h < 2/k).

conditions.title: BIG-O, BIG-OMEGA, BIG-THETA
conditions.text:
SIMPLIFICATION RULES
     1. Drop constant factors: 5n = O(n).
     2. Keep only the dominant (fastest-growing) term:
        3n^2 + 5n + 2 = O(n^2).
     3. Sequential blocks: costs ADD -> O(max of the two).
     4. Nested loops: costs MULTIPLY.
     5. Different inputs need different variables: a loop over list A then
        a loop over list B is O(a + b), nested is O(a * b), not O(n).
     6. Logarithm bases do not matter: log_2 n = log_10 n / log_10 2 differs
        by a constant: O(log n).
     7. Big-O is an upper bound, so n = O(n^2) is TRUE but uninformative;
        prefer the tightest bound (Theta).

conditions.title: SIMPLE HASH FUNCTION AND LOAD FACTOR
conditions.text:
COLLISION RESOLUTION
   CHAINING: each bucket holds a list of entries. Expected chain length
        = alpha, so expected lookup time = O(1 + alpha).
   OPEN ADDRESSING: probe for another free slot in the array itself
        (linear probing: try h, h+1, h+2, ... mod m). Needs alpha < 1;
        performance degrades sharply as alpha -> 1; deletion needs
        tombstones.
   RESIZING: when alpha exceeds a threshold (e.g. 0.7), allocate a bigger
        table and rehash all keys (cost O(n), amortized O(1) per insert).

conditions.title: BINARY SEARCH TREE (BST) PROPERTY
conditions.text:
the property applies to entire subtrees, not just to
   direct children. Checking only parent-child relations misses
   violations: a node whose right grandchild is smaller than the
   ancestor is NOT valid.

conditions.title: HEIGHT AND NODE-COUNT RELATIONSHIPS
conditions.text:
the counts apply to binary trees; a tree whose levels are
   all full is perfect; an AVL tree guarantees height at most about 1.44
   log2(n + 2).

conditions.title: ARRAY REPRESENTATION (0-based indexing)
conditions.text:
valid for a COMPLETE binary tree stored level by level;
   1-based and 0-based formulas differ.

conditions.title: LOWER BOUND FOR COMPARISON SORTING
conditions.text:
applies to algorithms that only compare items; counting
   sort and radix sort escape the bound by using key values.

conditions.title: MERGE SORT COMPLEXITY (RECURRENCE)
conditions.text:
the merge step is linear. Always O(n log n) (best,
   average, worst). Extra space O(n). STABLE.
   MASTER THEOREM [SUPPLEMENTARY]: for T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n) with
   f(n) = Theta(n^d): if d < log_b a: T = Theta(n^(log_b a));
   if d = log_b a: T = Theta(n^d log n); if d > log_b a: T = Theta(n^d).
   Examples: 2T(n/2) + n -> n log n; T(n/2) + 1 -> log n (binary
   search); 2T(n/2) + 1 -> n; 4T(n/2) + n -> n^2.

conditions.title: THE STANDARD LAWS  (hold for all Boolean A, B, C)
conditions.text:
applies to two-valued logic. SQL has THREE values (TRUE,
   FALSE, UNKNOWN from NULL), where some laws (excluded middle
   A OR ~A = TRUE) fail for NULL.
   !! WARNING !! The second distributive law A v (B ^ C) = (A v B) ^ (A v C)
   has NO analog in ordinary arithmetic (a + bc is not (a+b)(a+c));
   students often forget it holds in Boolean algebra.

conditions.title: DE MORGAN'S LAWS
conditions.text:
two-valued logic (in SQL with NULL, three-valued logic
   needs care: NOT of an unknown value is unknown).

conditions.title: THE CORE OPERATORS
conditions.text:
set operators need union-compatible relations; natural
   join needs common attribute names; the pure model has no duplicate
   rows, SQL does.

conditions.title: JOIN ALGORITHMS AND THEIR COST (R with r rows, S with s rows)
conditions.text:
hash join needs equality conditions; sort-merge handles
   ranges; indexes help selective joins.

conditions.title: DISTRIBUTIVE AGGREGATES
conditions.text:
empty partitions must send the identity element (count 0,
   sum 0, min = +infinity, max = -infinity); NULLs excluded consistently.

conditions.title: GLOBAL MEAN FROM PARTITION MEANS
conditions.text:
weights non-negative with positive sum; the local means must
   be over the SAME quantity. Weights are sample sizes for means; for
   other statistics the weights may differ.

conditions.title: COMBINING VARIANCES (SUM-OF-SQUARES FORM)
conditions.text:
& NUMERICAL WARNING: this form suffers CATASTROPHIC
   CANCELLATION when the mean is large relative to the spread (Q/N and
   mu^2 are huge and nearly equal; subtracting loses precision and can
   even produce a negative variance). Use the stable form below for real
   systems.

conditions.title: COMBINING VARIANCES (STABLE, PARALLEL / CHAN ET AL. FORM)
conditions.text: exact (up to floating point); numerically stable.

conditions.title: THE HALTING PROBLEM
conditions.text:
the result concerns the GENERAL problem over ALL programs and
   inputs. Individual programs can often be analyzed (simple loops
   with a decreasing counter provably halt). The theorem says no single
   method works for all.

conditions.title: DETERMINISTIC FINITE AUTOMATON (DFA)
conditions.text:
DFA recognition takes O(|w|) time and O(1) memory. Finite
   memory is the key limitation (27.6). A "dead/trap" state is used for
   impossible continuations if delta is to be total.

conditions.title: NONDETERMINISTIC FINITE AUTOMATON (NFA)
conditions.text:
THEOREM: NFAs and DFAs recognize exactly the same languages. SUBSET
   CONSTRUCTION converts an n-state NFA into a DFA with up to 2^n states.
   The blow-up can really occur.

conditions.title: REGULAR EXPRESSIONS (theoretical syntax)
conditions.text:
theoretical regular expressions have only union,
   concatenation and star; practical engines add features
   (backreferences, lookahead) that exceed regular languages.

conditions.title: PUMPING LEMMA FOR REGULAR LANGUAGES
conditions.text:
it is a NECESSARY condition for regularity. It can be used
   only to PROVE NON-regularity (via contrapositive). Passing the test
   does NOT prove a language regular.
   HOW TO USE (a game): (1) assume L regular with pumping length p;
   (2) YOU choose a clever string w in L with |w| >= p; (3) for ANY split
   x y z satisfying (1) and (2), (4) find i with x y^i z not in L;
   (5) contradiction.

conditions.title: AMDAHL'S LAW
conditions.text:
fixed problem size; ignores communication, load imbalance
   and overheads (real speed-ups are lower). If the problem grows with
   the machine, Gustafson's law S = (1 - f) + f p [SUPPLEMENTARY] is the
   more relevant model.

conditions.title: ARITHMETIC MEAN
conditions.text:
needs numeric (interval/ratio) data. It uses every value, so
   it is SENSITIVE TO OUTLIERS (breakdown point 0: a single extreme
   value can move it arbitrarily).
   KEY PROPERTIES
     (1) sum (x_i - x_bar) = 0  (deviations balance).
     (2) x_bar minimizes sum (x_i - c)^2 over c (least squares).
     (3) Linear: mean(a x + b) = a x_bar + b.
     (4) mean(x + y) = mean(x) + mean(y) for paired data.

conditions.title: WEIGHTED MEAN
conditions.text:
weights must be meaningful (credits, group sizes, inverse
   variances). Class midpoints in grouped data give an APPROXIMATION.

conditions.title: MEDIAN
conditions.text:
needs at least ordinal data. For even n, the average of the two
   middle values may not be an observed value (for discrete or categorical
   ordinal data some use the lower or upper median).

conditions.title: DENSITY HISTOGRAM
conditions.text:
with UNEQUAL bin widths a count histogram is misleading (a
   wide bin looks tall merely because it is wide); use density heights.

conditions.title: EMPIRICAL CUMULATIVE DISTRIBUTION FUNCTION (ECDF)
conditions.text:
right-continuous, non-decreasing, between 0 and 1. By the
   Glivenko-Cantelli theorem [SUPPLEMENTARY] F_n converges uniformly to the
   true CDF F as n grows. Quantiles are read by inverting F_n.

conditions.title: SKEWNESS COEFFICIENTS
conditions.text:
skewness is sensitive to outliers; needs adequate n
   (unstable for small samples); several definitions exist, so state
   which one.

conditions.title: RANGE
conditions.text:
needs numeric data; it grows with sample size and is
   dominated by outliers.

conditions.title: INTERQUARTILE RANGE (IQR)
conditions.text:
needs a stated quartile convention; robust to outliers
   (breakdown point 25%).

conditions.title: POPULATION VARIANCE AND STANDARD DEVIATION
conditions.text:
use when the data are the ENTIRE population of interest.
   Properties: sigma^2 >= 0 (= 0 iff all values equal); Var(a x + b) =
   a^2 Var(x) (shifting does not matter, scaling squares);
   units of variance are squared units; SD has the original units.

conditions.title: SAMPLE VARIANCE AND SAMPLE STANDARD DEVIATION
conditions.text:
needs n >= 2. Assumes the sample is random from the
   population. s^2 is UNBIASED for sigma^2 (E[s^2] = sigma^2); s is NOT
   unbiased for sigma (slightly underestimates, by Jensen's inequality,
   because sqrt is concave).

conditions.title: COVARIANCE
PEARSON CORRELATION COEFFICIENT
conditions.text:
& PROPERTIES
     - Measures LINEAR association only.
     - r = +1 or -1 iff all points lie exactly on a straight line (positive or
       negative slope); r = 0 means NO LINEAR association (not
       independence).
     - Symmetric: r(X, Y) = r(Y, X).
     - Needs non-zero variance in both variables.
     - Sensitive to outliers and to restricted range (selecting only high
       values of x lowers r).
     - In simple linear regression r^2 = R^2, the share of variance of y
       explained by x; slope b1 = r s_y / s_x.

conditions.title: INVARIANCE OF CORRELATION UNDER LINEAR TRANSFORMATIONS
conditions.text:
holds exactly for linear changes of units; not for
   nonlinear transformations.

conditions.title: PROBABILITY AXIOMS (KOLMOGOROV) AND CONSEQUENCES
conditions.text:
HOW PROBABILITIES ARE ASSIGNED
     CLASSICAL (equally likely outcomes, finite Omega):
         P(A) = |A| / |Omega|  (number of favorable / total outcomes).
         Valid ONLY if the outcomes are genuinely equally likely.
     EMPIRICAL (relative frequency): P(A) approx (times A occurred)/(number
         of trials), converging as trials grow (law of large numbers).
     SUBJECTIVE: degree of belief (Bayesian).

conditions.title: COMPLEMENT RULE
conditions.text:
always valid; for 'at least one of independent events'
   use 1 minus the product of the (1 - p_i).

conditions.title: ADDITION RULE
conditions.text: always valid (the disjoint form needs mutual exclusivity).

conditions.title: MULTIPLICATION RULE (INTRODUCTION)
conditions.text:
INDEPENDENCE must be justified (separate coin tosses: yes; two cards
   drawn without replacement: no). The multiplication rule with
   conditional probabilities is the general form.

conditions.title: FUNDAMENTAL COUNTING PRINCIPLES
conditions.text:
the number of options at a later stage must not depend on
   earlier choices (otherwise count case by case).

conditions.title: PERMUTATIONS
conditions.text: distinct objects for the first two formulas; 0 <= k <= n.

conditions.title: COMBINATIONS
conditions.text: 0 <= k <= n; selections without repetition (basic version).

conditions.title: PROBABILITY FOR SAMPLING WITHOUT REPLACEMENT (HYPERGEOMETRIC)
conditions.text:
equally likely samples (random draw); without replacement.
   If n is small relative to N (rule of thumb n < 0.05 N or 0.1 N) the
   binomial approximation (Module 35) is adequate.

conditions.title: CONDITIONAL PROBABILITY
conditions.text:
requires P(B) > 0. Conditional probabilities obey all the
   axioms (e.g. P(A^c | B) = 1 - P(A | B)). In general P(A | B) != P(B | A).

conditions.title: INDEPENDENCE
conditions.text:
independence is an ASSUMPTION to be justified (by the physical
   process, e.g. separate dice, or tested from data), not something to
   assume because the events "feel unrelated".

conditions.title: GENERAL MULTIPLICATION (CHAIN) RULE
conditions.text:
always valid; simplifies to a product of unconditional
   probabilities when events are independent.

conditions.title: LAW OF TOTAL PROBABILITY
conditions.text:
the B_i MUST partition the whole space (no gaps, no
   overlaps), and the weights sum to 1.

conditions.title: BAYES' THEOREM
conditions.text:
P(B) > 0; priors must be meaningful and sum to 1 over the
   partition. The posterior is only as good as the prior and the
   likelihood model.

conditions.title: PREDICTIVE VALUES FROM SENSITIVITY, SPECIFICITY AND PREVALENCE
conditions.text:
assumes sensitivity and specificity are the same across
   the population and that Pr is the prevalence in the population where
   the test is applied.

conditions.title: RANDOM VARIABLE
conditions.text:
X must be a function for which P(X <= x) is defined; its
   type (discrete or continuous) determines how probabilities are
   described.

conditions.title: PMF
conditions.text:
only for discrete variables; each p(x) is a genuine probability
   (between 0 and 1).

conditions.title: PDF
conditions.text:
the density must integrate to 1 (normalization); non-negative;
   improper integrals must converge (Module 4). Distinguish the density
   f(x) (not a probability) from the probability P(X = x) = 0 for any
   single x (Module 36).

conditions.title: CDF
conditions.text:
F always exists; it is right-continuous; for continuous X
   it is continuous, for discrete X it jumps.

conditions.title: CONTINUOUS UNIFORM DISTRIBUTION U(a, b)
conditions.text: bounded support; values outside [a, b] impossible.

conditions.title: BERNOULLI(p)
conditions.text: exactly two outcomes with fixed probability p.

conditions.title: BINOMIAL(n, p)
conditions.text:
(BINS): Binary outcome per trial; Independent trials;
   Number of trials fixed in advance; Same probability p on every trial.
   Violations: sampling WITHOUT replacement from a small population
   (hypergeometric instead); p changing over time; clustered/dependent
   data; unknown n.

conditions.title: NORMAL DISTRIBUTION N(mu, sigma^2)
conditions.text:
a MODEL; real data are only approximately normal. Check with
   histograms, Q-Q plots, tests. Heavy-tailed data (financial returns)
   violate it. Sum rule: if X ~ N(mu1, s1^2) and Y ~ N(mu2, s2^2) are
   independent then X + Y ~ N(mu1 + mu2, s1^2 + s2^2) (VARIANCES add, not
   SDs); aX + b ~ N(a mu + b, a^2 sigma^2).

conditions.title: EXPONENTIAL(lambda)
conditions.text:
constant rate, independent events; support x >= 0. Real
   lifetimes often have increasing/decreasing hazard (use Weibull
   etc.). The exponential is the only continuous distribution with the
   memoryless property.

conditions.title: EXPECTED VALUE (MEAN) OF A RANDOM VARIABLE
conditions.text:
the sum/integral must converge absolutely. Counterexample:
   the Cauchy distribution (f(x) = 1/(pi(1 + x^2))) has NO mean (F4.8).
   In general E[g(X)] != g(E[X]); for CONVEX g Jensen's inequality gives
   E[g(X)] >= g(E[X]).

conditions.title: LINEARITY OF EXPECTATION
conditions.text:
holds ALWAYS for sums (the strength of the theorem); the
   product rule needs independence (or zero covariance).

conditions.title: VARIANCE
conditions.text:
needs a finite second moment. Variances add only when
   covariances vanish (otherwise include 2 Cov). Standard deviations do
   NOT add.

conditions.title: MOMENTS AND THE MOMENT GENERATING FUNCTION
conditions.text:
higher moments may not exist for heavy-tailed distributions
   (Cauchy: none; Student t with 3 degrees of freedom: no 4th moment).

conditions.title: LINEAR AND NONLINEAR TRANSFORMATIONS
conditions.text:
the density formula needs g monotone on the support (else
   split into monotone pieces and add contributions). Expectation of a
   nonlinear transform: use LOTUS, not g(E[X]).

conditions.title: INTERVAL PROBABILITIES
conditions.text:
for continuous X the endpoints are irrelevant; for
   discrete X they matter.

conditions.title: SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION OF A STATISTIC
conditions.text: it depends on the population, the sampling scheme and n.

conditions.title: MEAN AND VARIANCE OF THE SAMPLE MEAN
conditions.text:
independence (clustered or serially correlated data have a
   larger variance of x_bar). If sampling WITHOUT replacement from a finite
   population: Var(x_bar) = (sigma^2/n) (N - n)/(N - 1), the FINITE
   POPULATION CORRECTION (fpc); negligible when n << N.

conditions.title: LAW OF LARGE NUMBERS (LLN)
conditions.text:
PROOF IDEA (Chebyshev): P(|x_bar - mu| > eps) <= Var(x_bar)/eps^2 =
   sigma^2/(n eps^2) -> 0.

conditions.title: CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM (CLT)
conditions.text:
& CAUTIONS
   - Independence and finite variance (the Cauchy distribution has no
     variance: its sample mean is as variable as one observation).
   - The speed of convergence depends on the population: symmetric
     distributions converge quickly; heavily skewed ones need larger n.
     Rule of thumb n >= 30 (not a law).
   - The CLT is about the distribution of the MEAN (or sum), NOT about the
     data becoming normal.
   - Proportions: p_hat approx N(p, p(1 - p)/n) when n p >= 10 and
     n(1 - p) >= 10 (the binomial CLT).

conditions.title: BIAS AND UNBIASED ESTIMATORS
conditions.text:
unbiasedness refers to the sampling distribution, with the
   model assumptions (e.g. iid). It is NOT sufficient for a good
   estimator (see variance) nor necessary (see MSE).

conditions.title: VARIANCE OF AN ESTIMATOR, EFFICIENCY AND MSE
conditions.text:
MSE needs finite second moments; the decomposition holds
   for any estimator with finite variance.

conditions.title: CONSISTENCY
conditions.text:
a large-sample property; bias tending to 0 and variance
   tending to 0 is sufficient.

conditions.title: STANDARD ERROR
conditions.text:
the formulas assume iid sampling (no clustering/serial
   correlation); sigma replaced by s adds uncertainty (t distribution
   for small n).

conditions.title: METHOD OF MOMENTS
conditions.text:
needs finite moments; the resulting estimates may lie
   outside the allowed parameter space; MoM estimators are consistent but
   usually less efficient than MLEs.

conditions.title: LIKELIHOOD FUNCTION
MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD ESTIMATOR
conditions.text:
model correctly specified (family); iid (or specified
   dependence); the maximum may lie on the boundary of the parameter space
   (derivative methods fail, see uniform below); the likelihood may have
   several local maxima (mixtures, neural nets) or none.

conditions.title: FISHER INFORMATION AND THE CRAMER-RAO BOUND
conditions.text:
regularity conditions (smooth model, support independent
   of theta, interior parameter); the bound applies to unbiased
   estimators; asymptotic results need large n.

conditions.title: IDENTIFIABILITY
SIGNIFICANCE LEVEL ALPHA
conditions.text:
