alpha is a threshold set by the analyst based on the cost of
   false positives (drug approval: small; exploratory screening: larger).
   0.05 is a convention, not a law of nature.

conditions.title: GENERAL FORM OF A TEST STATISTIC
conditions.text:
the null distribution of the statistic must be known
   (normal, t, chi-square, F), which requires the test's assumptions.

conditions.title: z-TEST FOR A MEAN (sigma known, or large n)
conditions.text:
random sample; population normal OR n large (CLT); sigma known
   (rare in practice).

conditions.title: t-STATISTIC (sigma unknown)
conditions.text:
independent observations; population approximately normal (or n
   large; t is fairly robust except with strong skew or outliers in
   small samples).

conditions.title: p-VALUE
conditions.text:
p-values are valid only if the model/assumptions behind the
   null distribution hold and the test was specified in advance. If H0 is
   true and the test statistic is continuous, p is UNIFORMLY distributed on
   (0, 1): a p-value below 0.05 happens 5% of the time by design
   (simulation with 5,000 t-tests on null data gives 5.1%).

conditions.title: ERROR RATES AND POWER
conditions.text:
power is computed for a specific alternative; the
   formulas shown are for the z-test with known sigma (approximate for
   t-tests).

conditions.title: CONFIDENCE INTERVAL FOR A MEAN
conditions.text:
same as the corresponding test (random sample, near-normal
   or large n). Wald proportion intervals need n p_hat >= 10 and
   n(1 - p_hat) >= 10; otherwise use Wilson or exact methods.

conditions.title: THE THREE t-TESTS
conditions.text:
see 39.8. CHOOSE the test by the DESIGN: same units measured
   twice -> paired; two separate groups -> two-sample.

conditions.title: THE SIMPLE LINEAR REGRESSION MODEL
conditions.text:
see 40.7 (assumptions). Regression describes the average
   relationship; it does not by itself say that x causes y (40.9).

conditions.title: LEAST SQUARES ESTIMATES FOR SIMPLE REGRESSION
conditions.text:
needs variation in x (S_xx > 0); outliers and leverage points
   strongly affect it.

conditions.title: GOODNESS OF FIT: SST, SSR, SSE AND R^2
conditions.text:
SST = SSR + SSE requires OLS with an intercept; R^2 can
   be negative for predictions on new data.

conditions.title: INFERENCE FOR THE SLOPE AND INTERCEPT
conditions.text:
the assumptions of 40.7 (normal errors for exact t inference;
   otherwise approximate by the CLT).

conditions.title: PREDICTION: MEAN RESPONSE vs NEW OBSERVATION
conditions.text:
assumes the model assumptions of section 40.7;
   extrapolation voids the guarantee.

conditions.title: MULTIPLE LINEAR REGRESSION
conditions.text:
n > p + 1; X has FULL COLUMN RANK (no perfect collinearity,
   Modules 8 and 38); the assumptions of 40.7. Practical: standardize
   predictors for numerical stability/interpretation; use QR/SVD
   (np.linalg.lstsq) rather than inverting X^T X.

conditions.title: LEVERAGE AND COOK'S DISTANCE
conditions.text:
the thresholds are rules of thumb; compare with the
   distribution of the diagnostics.

conditions.title: MULTICOLLINEARITY AND THE VARIANCE INFLATION FACTOR
conditions.text:
CONSEQUENCES: coefficient estimates have HIGH VARIANCE (change wildly with
   small data changes; signs may flip); individual t-tests insignificant
   although the overall F-test and R^2 are strong; interpretation of
   single coefficients unreliable. NOT affected: the fitted values and
   predictions within the range of the collinear pattern, and the
   overall R^2. Predictions break when new data violate the collinear
   pattern.

conditions.title: OMITTED VARIABLE BIAS
conditions.text:
bias exists only if x_2 affects y AND is correlated with
   x_1; the formula is exact in the large-sample limit.

conditions.title: FEATURE SCALING FORMULAS
conditions.text:
choose by distribution: standardization for roughly
   symmetric data; min-max is sensitive to outliers (a single extreme value
   squeezes everything else); robust scaling tolerates outliers. Apply the
   SAME training-set constants to new data. Do not scale the target for
   trees unnecessarily; remember to invert transformations of y when
   reporting.
   !! DENOMINATOR CONVENTION !! sklearn StandardScaler divides by the
   POPULATION sd (ddof = 0); pandas .std() uses ddof = 1.

conditions.title: CONVEX FUNCTIONS
conditions.text:
EXAMPLES: convex: x^2, e^x, |x|, x ln x, MSE for linear models (Hessian
   (2/n) X^T X is PSD), logistic loss, hinge loss, ridge objective.
   NON-convex: x^4 - 3x^2 + x, neural-network losses, k-means objective,
   mixture-model likelihoods.

conditions.title: GRADIENT DESCENT (GD)
conditions.text:
f differentiable; eta must be small enough (see below); finds a
   stationary point: global minimum for convex f, otherwise only a local
   minimum or saddle point (43.6). Each iteration costs one gradient.

conditions.title: NEWTON-RAPHSON FOR ROOT FINDING (ONE VARIABLE)
conditions.text:
f'(x_n) != 0; start reasonably close to the root; convergence
   is QUADRATIC near a simple root (the number of correct digits roughly
   doubles each step). Can diverge, cycle, or jump to another root
   from a poor start.

conditions.title: NEWTON'S METHOD FOR OPTIMIZATION (MULTIVARIATE)
conditions.text:
needs the Hessian (expensive: d^2 entries, O(d^3) to solve);
   the Hessian must be positive definite near the solution, otherwise
   the step may point uphill or toward a saddle (modify H: add lambda I,
   trust regions, line search). Pure Newton may diverge far from the
   optimum. Local convergence is quadratic.
   Practical variants: QUASI-NEWTON (BFGS, L-BFGS build a Hessian
   approximation from gradients), Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt
   (nonlinear least squares), IRLS (logistic regression).

conditions.title: NELDER-MEAD (DOWNHILL SIMPLEX)
conditions.text:
use for noisy, non-differentiable or "black-box" objectives
   with few parameters (about 2-10). It may stall at non-stationary points,
   has no general convergence guarantee, and becomes very slow as the
   dimension grows. Sensitive to the initial simplex and to scaling.

conditions.title: CLASS PROPORTIONS AND PREDICTION
conditions.text:
leaves with few cases give unreliable proportions (a leaf
   with 1 observation says "probability 1.0"): regularize (min samples
   per leaf) or smooth (Laplace correction (n_k + 1)/(n + K)). Predicted
   probabilities from a single deep tree are poorly calibrated.

conditions.title: GINI IMPURITY
conditions.text: needs class proportions; for K classes the maximum is 1 - 1/K.

conditions.title: ENTROPY
conditions.text: p_k = 0 terms contribute 0.

conditions.title: INFORMATION GAIN (IMPURITY DECREASE)
conditions.text:
Gain >= 0 for concave impurities. Gain favours splits
   producing many tiny children (e.g. an ID column): use binary splits,
   minimum leaf sizes, or the gain ratio (C4.5) to counter this.

conditions.title: SPLITTING CRITERION FOR REGRESSION TREES
conditions.text:
numeric target; outliers dominate squared error (use
   absolute-error criteria for robustness).

conditions.title: COST-COMPLEXITY PRUNING
conditions.text:
alpha is chosen by cross-validation; the nested sequence
   of subtrees comes from weakest-link pruning.

conditions.title: BOOTSTRAP SAMPLE
conditions.text:
the 36.8% is a large-n limit; for small n the exact value
   is (1 - 1/n)^n.

conditions.title: BAGGING (BOOTSTRAP AGGREGATING)
conditions.text:
helps unstable (high-variance) learners such as deep
   trees, little for stable ones.

conditions.title: VARIANCE OF AN AVERAGE OF CORRELATED PREDICTORS
conditions.text:
assumes equal variance and a common pairwise correlation
   across trees (an idealization); rho is typically positive.

conditions.title: OUT-OF-BAG ERROR
conditions.text:
needs enough trees (B large) so every observation is OOB for
   several trees; slightly pessimistic for small B (each OOB prediction
   uses fewer trees); unbiased only if the model/hyperparameters were
   NOT tuned on the same OOB score (tuning on it makes it optimistic;
   Module 47). It is not valid for dependent data without care (grouped/time
   series).

conditions.title: BIAS-VARIANCE DECOMPOSITION OF EXPECTED TEST ERROR
conditions.text:
holds for squared-error loss with additive noise
   independent of the model; analogous decompositions exist for other
   losses.

conditions.title: K-FOLD CROSS-VALIDATION
conditions.text:
observations should be (approximately) exchangeable; for
   dependent data use GROUP k-fold or TIME-SERIES splits. The model is
   RETRAINED within each fold (all preprocessing inside the loop; see
   leakage). The final model is refit on ALL data after selection.
   BIAS-VARIANCE OF THE ESTIMATOR: small k (2-3) trains on much less data
   than the final model (pessimistic bias); large k (LOOCV) has low bias
   but higher variance and cost; k = 5-10 is a good compromise.

conditions.title: CONFUSION MATRIX AND DERIVED CLASSIFICATION METRICS
conditions.text:
choose the metric from the business cost; accuracy is
   misleading when classes are imbalanced.

conditions.title: THRESHOLDS, ROC CURVE AND AUC
conditions.text:
needs scores that rank cases; AUC ignores calibration and
   class prevalence.

conditions.title: LOG-LOSS (CROSS-ENTROPY) AND CALIBRATION
conditions.text:
probabilities must lie in (0, 1) (clip to avoid ln 0);
   the multi-class version uses -ln p(true class).

conditions.title: REGRESSION METRICS
conditions.text:
R^2 on new data compares with the training-mean baseline
   and can be negative; MAPE needs y != 0.

conditions.title: GRID SEARCH
conditions.text:
cost grows EXPONENTIALLY with the number of hyperparameters
   (the curse of dimensionality): 5 values for each of 4 hyperparameters =
   625 configurations; with 5-fold CV = 3,125 fits. The grid resolution
   is fixed: the optimum may lie between grid points, and for each
   hyperparameter only m_i distinct values are explored.

conditions.title: RANDOM SEARCH
conditions.text:
gives no guarantee of finding the optimum; results vary with
   the seed; with a good prior range it finds near-optimal settings
   quickly. The chance that at least one of n random draws lands in the
   top fraction q of the space is 1 - (1 - q)^n: for the best 5% and n =
   60: 1 - 0.95^60 = 95.4%.

conditions.title: NESTED CROSS-VALIDATION
conditions.text:
the final deployable model is then obtained by running the
   tuning procedure once more on ALL the data. Nested CV is needed when the
   tuned score will be REPORTED or used to compare model families; for
   merely picking hyperparameters, plain CV suffices.
   Slightly pessimistic bias is possible (inner models use less data).

conditions.title: LINEAR CLASSIFIER AND ITS DECISION BOUNDARY
conditions.text:
only LINEARLY SEPARABLE (or approximately separable) classes
   can be classified well. For perfectly separable data the unpenalized
   logistic MLE does not exist (coefficients diverge, Module 43.8): use
   regularization. Features should be scaled for regularized models.

conditions.title: THE XOR PROBLEM
conditions.text:
the argument is for linear classifiers on the two raw
   features; an added interaction or a hidden layer changes the
   hypothesis space.

conditions.title: LINEAR DISCRIMINANT ANALYSIS
conditions.text:
Gaussian classes with equal covariances (checked by
   within-class scatter plots, Box's M test, or just by performance);
   n > p (or use SHRINKAGE: solver = "lsqr", shrinkage = "auto"); sensitive
   to outliers; linear boundary. If covariances differ: QUADRATIC
   DISCRIMINANT ANALYSIS (QDA): class-specific Sigma_k, boundaries are
   quadratic curves, more parameters, needs more data.

conditions.title: INTERACTIONS BETWEEN FEATURES
conditions.text:
CAUTIONS: main effects alone may mislead when an interaction exists;
   include main effects when including their product; interaction terms
   increase collinearity (center variables first, Module 40.6) and the
   number of parameters (p(p-1)/2 pairs).

conditions.title: KERNEL FUNCTIONS AND THE KERNEL TRICK
HARD-MARGIN SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINE
conditions.text:
only for linearly separable data; otherwise use the soft
   margin (F48.7).

conditions.title: SOFT-MARGIN SVM, THE PARAMETER C AND REGULARIZATION
conditions.text:
standardize features; choose C (and kernel parameters) by
   cross-validation on a log grid (Module 47); training cost grows between
   O(n^2) and O(n^3), so SVMs suit small/medium data (use linear SVM /
   SGD for very large n). Outputs are scores, not probabilities (Platt
   scaling adds them).

  Closed form          usually easy                often, sometimes not
  Efficiency           often lower                 asymptotically optimal
  Infeasible values    possible (uniform example)  respects the parameter space
  Bias                 can be biased               can be biased (normal variance)
  Computation          solve equations             optimization (Module 43)
  Use                  quick/starting values       standard in practice (GLMs,
                                                   neural net losses)

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: TYPE I vs TYPE II ERROR
tables.rawText:
Aspect         Type I                      Type II
  Meaning        reject a TRUE H0            fail to reject a FALSE H0
  Also called    false positive, false alarm false negative, miss
  Probability    alpha (set by analyst)      beta (depends on effect, n, alpha)
  Control        choose alpha                increase n, effect, reduce noise
  Trade-off      lowering alpha raises beta (for fixed n)
  Example        declaring a useless drug    missing a useful drug
                 effective                   (confirming it is "no different")
  ML analog      false positive rate         false negative rate (1 - recall)

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: SIMPLE vs MULTIPLE LINEAR REGRESSION
tables.rawText:
Aspect             Simple                      Multiple
  Predictors         one                         p >= 2
  Geometry           line in (x, y) plane        hyperplane
  Slope meaning      total association           effect holding others fixed
  Estimation         b_1 = S_xy/S_xx             (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y
  R^2                = r^2                       use adjusted R^2
  Residual df        n - 2                       n - p - 1
  Main risk          omitted variables           multicollinearity, overfitting
  Slope in presence  can differ markedly from the coefficient once other
  of other variables variables are included (Simpson's paradox is the extreme)

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: OUTLIER vs LEVERAGE vs INFLUENCE
tables.rawText:
Concept        Extreme in...        Measure             Effect on fit
  Outlier        y given x (residual) studentized resid.  inflates sigma_hat; may
                                                          not move the slope if x is central
  High leverage  x (predictor space)  h_ii                potential to pull; may be harmless
                                                          if it lies on the trend
  Influential    combination          Cook's D, DFBETAS   changes coefficients/predictions
  Typical cases  (low lev., big resid) = outlier only; (high lev., on the trend) = leverage only;
                 (high lev., off the trend) = influential

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: GRADIENT DESCENT vs NEWTON'S METHOD
tables.rawText:
Aspect                Gradient descent               Newton's method
  Information used      gradient (first order)         gradient + Hessian (second order)
  Update                theta - eta g                  theta - H^(-1) g
  Step size             needs tuned eta                determined by curvature
  Cost per iteration    O(d) (one gradient)            O(d^2) memory, O(d^3) solve
  Iterations needed     many (linear rate, depends     few (quadratic rate near solution)
                        on kappa)
  Convergence           global for small eta (convex)  local; may diverge from poor start
  Sensitive to scale    yes (condition number)         invariant to linear rescaling
  Non-convex behavior   moves downhill always          may move toward saddles/maxima
  Large-scale use       standard (SGD, Adam)           limited; use L-BFGS / quasi-Newton
  Example               training neural nets           logistic regression (IRLS),
                                                       small/medium smooth problems

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: GINI vs ENTROPY
tables.rawText:
Aspect            Gini impurity               Entropy / information gain
  Formula           1 - sum p_k^2               -sum p_k log2 p_k
  Maximum (K = 2)   0.5                         1 bit
  Computation       cheaper (no logs)           slightly slower
  Behavior          similar; tends to isolate   tends to produce slightly more
                    the most frequent class     balanced splits
  Default           scikit-learn "gini"         criterion="entropy" or "log_loss"
  Practical effect  usually negligible difference in accuracy
  Misclassification error 1 - max p_k is less sensitive: used for pruning, not for growing.

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: BAGGING vs BOOSTING
tables.rawText:
Aspect              Bagging / random forest          Boosting
     Training            independent trees (parallel)     sequential, each corrects the last
     Data per model      bootstrap sample                 re-weighted or residuals
     Base learners       deep, low-bias, high-variance    shallow, high-bias trees
     Main effect         reduces variance                 reduces bias (and some variance)
     Overfitting risk    low; more trees do not overfit   can overfit with too many rounds
     Tuning              few hyperparameters, robust      learning rate, rounds, depth matter
     Parallelism         easy (n_jobs)                    limited
     Examples            RandomForest, ExtraTrees         AdaBoost, GradientBoosting, XGBoost

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: SINGLE TREE vs RANDOM FOREST
tables.rawText:
Aspect             Single decision tree        Random forest
  Variance           high (unstable)             low (averaged)
  Bias               low if deep                 about the same as one deep tree
  Interpretability   high (rules)                low (use importances)
  Training cost      one tree                    B trees (parallel)
  Prediction         one path                    B paths + vote/average
  Overfitting        severe if unpruned          resistant; more trees safe
  Validation         needs held-out/CV           OOB available free
  Typical accuracy   baseline                    usually clearly better

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: TRAINING ERROR vs TEST ERROR
tables.rawText:
Aspect              Training error               Test error
  Data                data used to fit the model   fresh data, untouched by fitting/tuning
  Tends to be         optimistic (too low)         honest (unbiased) estimate
  As complexity rises always decreases (memorizes) U-shaped: falls, then rises
  Use                 diagnose underfitting;       report performance; compare
                      monitor optimization         final models
  Danger              mistaking it for quality     reusing test set repeatedly

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: PARAMETERS vs HYPERPARAMETERS
tables.rawText:
Aspect            Model parameters                 Hyperparameters
  Meaning           numbers LEARNED from data        settings chosen BEFORE/around training
  Set by            the training algorithm           the analyst or a tuning procedure
                    (OLS, gradient descent)          (grid/random search, CV)
  Examples          regression coefficients,         learning rate, tree depth, number of
                    tree split thresholds, neural    trees, k in k-NN, ridge lambda, SVM C
                    network weights, class priors    and gamma, batch size, epochs
  Optimized on      training loss                    validation (CV) score
  How many          from a few to billions           typically 2-10
  Stored in         fitted model (coef_, tree_)      constructor arguments (get_params)
  Effect            define the fitted function       control complexity/behavior
                                                     (bias-variance trade-off)
  Example (ridge)   beta (learned)                   lambda (the penalty weight)
  Example (forest)  split features/thresholds        n_estimators, max_features, max_depth
  KEY RULE: hyperparameters must NOT be chosen by minimizing TRAINING error
  (it always prefers the most flexible model); choose by validation/CV
  performance.
THE TWO-LEVEL VIEW: inner problem: for fixed hyperparameters h, find parameters
theta(h) that minimize the training loss; outer problem: find h that
minimizes the validation loss of theta(h). Tuning is optimization of a
noisy black-box function of h (no gradient available; expensive: every
evaluation trains a model).
SEARCH SPACES: the set of values to explore for each hyperparameter:
   - SCALE: use a LOG scale for hyperparameters spanning orders of
     magnitude (learning rate 1e-5 to 1; ridge lambda; SVM C 1e-2 to 1e3;
     gamma): sample log-uniformly (scipy loguniform) so that 0.001 and
     0.1 are equally likely to be explored.
   - TYPE: integers (depth 1-20), categorical (kernel linear/rbf),
     continuous (fraction), conditional (gamma only matters for the RBF
     kernel).
   - RANGE: wide enough to bracket the optimum (if the best value is at the
     boundary of the grid, extend the grid).
   - Start coarse and refine around good regions.

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: GRID vs RANDOM SEARCH
tables.rawText:
Aspect               Grid search                    Random search
  Candidates           fixed lattice                  random draws from distributions
  Cost                 product of list lengths        user budget n_iter
  Scales with d        exponentially                  independent of d
  Distinct values per  m_i                            n_iter (all distinct)
  hyperparameter
  Covers               regular but may miss between   irregular, good for important
                       points                         parameters
  Reproducibility      deterministic                  needs a seed
  Best when            1-2 hyperparameters, cheap     3+ hyperparameters, expensive
                       models                         models, continuous ranges

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: BOOTSTRAP vs CROSS-VALIDATION
tables.rawText:
Aspect            k-fold cross-validation        Bootstrap (out-of-bag)
  Resampling        partition: each case in test   draw n WITH replacement; test on cases
                    once                           not drawn (about 36.8%)
  Training size     (k-1)/k of n (80% for k = 5)   about 63.2% distinct cases
  Test cases        every case exactly once        each case in about 36.8% of replicates
  Bias              small pessimistic bias         pessimistic (less distinct data);
                                                   .632/.632+ corrections
  Variance          moderate; repeat to reduce     low with many replicates
  Typical use       model selection and comparison estimating uncertainty of a statistic
                                                   (SE, CI); OOB in forests
  Cost              k fits                          B fits (B = 100-1000+)
  Resubstitution error (training error) is the worst estimate: biased low.
  VERIFIED (200 training cases, random forest; truth from 19,800 fresh cases):
      resubstitution 1.000; 10-fold CV 0.895; bootstrap-OOB (100 replicates) 0.888;
      true accuracy 0.891. Both resampling estimates are close to the truth.
  RULE OF THUMB: CV for selecting/comparing models; the bootstrap for
  quantifying the uncertainty of an estimate (percentile CI) and for OOB
  inside bagged ensembles. For small samples, repeated CV or the .632+
  bootstrap are good.

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: CLASSIFICATION vs REGRESSION
tables.rawText:
Aspect              Classification                   Regression
  Target y            categorical (labels)             numeric (continuous)
  Output              class (and class probabilities)  a number (conditional mean)
  Loss                0-1 loss, log-loss/cross-entropy,   squared error, absolute error
                      hinge
  Metrics             accuracy, precision, recall,     RMSE, MAE, R^2
                      F1, AUC, log-loss
  Typical models      logistic regression, LDA, SVM,   linear regression, regression
                      trees, forests, k-NN             trees, SVR, ridge
  Decision object     decision boundary                fitted curve/surface
  Leaf/rule output    majority class                   mean
  Baseline            majority class                   mean of y
  Practical          class imbalance, thresholds,     heteroscedasticity, outliers,
  issues              calibration                      extrapolation
  Link: logistic "regression" is a CLASSIFICATION method (it models the
  probability of a class).

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: DECISION TREES vs LINEAR CLASSIFIERS
tables.rawText:
Aspect                  Decision tree/forest           Linear (logistic, LDA, lin. SVM)
  Boundary                axis-parallel boxes            one hyperplane
  Interactions            captured automatically         need explicit product terms
  Oblique boundaries      poor (staircase)               natural
  Nonlinear effects       yes (piecewise constant)       need transformations
  Feature scaling         not needed                     needed (regularized models)
  Interpretability        rules (tree); forest: low      coefficients, odds ratios
  Variance                high (single tree)             low (few parameters)
  Data requirement        more data for complex shapes   works with little data
  High dimension, p > n   can overfit, still works       works with regularization
  Extrapolation           constant beyond the data       linear continuation
  Probability output      step functions, uncalibrated   smooth (logistic)
  Missing values/types    handles mixed types, outliers  needs encoding/imputation
  Best when               tabular data, interactions,    approximately linear, many
                          mixed types                    features, small n, need coefficients
  Rule of thumb: start with a regularized linear baseline; try forests/boosting
  for tabular nonlinearity; kernels/NNs for smooth nonlinear structure.

tables.title: COMPARISON TABLE: LOSS FUNCTIONS FOR CLASSIFICATION (margin m = y f(x), y = +/-1)
tables.rawText:
Loss             Formula                    Convex?  Used by
  0-1 loss         1[m <= 0]                  no       evaluation (error rate)
  Hinge            max(0, 1 - m)              yes      SVM
  Logistic         ln(1 + e^(-m))             yes      logistic regression
  Squared          (1 - m)^2                  yes      least squares classifier / LDA
  Exponential      e^(-m)                     yes      AdaBoost
  The 0-1 loss is not differentiable and non-convex, so training uses smooth
  convex SURROGATES (Module 43); all penalize margins m < 1, but the
  logistic loss never becomes exactly zero (it keeps pushing the weights
  larger on separable data) while the hinge loss is exactly zero beyond the
  margin (sparse in support vectors).

definitions.title: 1.1 THE REAL NUMBER SYSTEM AND INTERVALS
definitions.text: Numbers come in nested families. Calculus works on the REAL numbers, which you can picture as every point on an infinitely long line with no gaps.

definitions.title: 1.3 ALGEBRAIC EXPRESSIONS AND SIMPLIFICATION
definitions.text: an equivalent but more useful form without changing its value. Every rule below is a statement "left side = right side for all allowed values".

definitions.title: 1.4 FUNCTIONS: DOMAIN, CODOMAIN AND RANGE
definitions.text: EXACTLY ONE output. A machine: put x in, get f(x) out; the same x always gives the same result.

definitions.title: 2.1 CONCEPT OF A LIMIT
definitions.text: A limit answers: "What value is f(x) getting closer and closer to as x gets closer and closer to a number a?" It is about the TREND near a, not the value AT a. The function does not even need to be defined at a.

definitions.title: 3.1 DERIVATIVES FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES
definitions.text: A derivative measures HOW FAST a quantity is changing at one exact instant. Average speed over a trip is "distance / time". But a speedometer shows speed AT A MOMENT. To get that, we take the average rate over a shorter and shorter time window and see what number it settles toward. That limiting number is the derivative.

definitions.title: 4.1 ANTIDERIVATIVES AND INDEFINITE INTEGRALS
definitions.text: Differentiation takes a function and gives its rate of change. Integration runs the film backwards: given a rate of change, rebuild the quantity. If a car's speed is known at every moment, integration gives the distance traveled.

definitions.title: 5.1 SEQUENCES AND CONVERGENCE
definitions.text: (a function from the positive integers). A sequence CONVERGES if its terms settle toward one number as the position n grows.

definitions.title: 6.1 SCALARS, VECTORS AND MATRICES
definitions.text: scalar : a single number (3, -0.5, pi). vector : an ordered list of numbers; can be a point or an arrow in space, or simply a data record (age, height, income). matrix : a rectangular grid of numbers; can be a table of data, or a machine that transforms vectors (rotate, stretch, project).

definitions.title: 8.1 VECTOR SPACES AND SUBSPACES
definitions.text: A vector space is a collection of "vectors" in which you can ADD any two and SCALE any one, and always land back inside the collection. R^n is the standard example. A subspace is a vector space sitting inside a bigger one (a line or plane through the origin inside R^3).

definitions.title: 9.1 EIGENVALUES AND EIGENVECTORS
definitions.text: Most vectors change direction when a matrix acts on them. A few special vectors only get STRETCHED or FLIPPED along their own line. Those are the eigenvectors; the stretch factor is the eigenvalue. They reveal the "natural axes" of the transformation.

definitions.title: 10.1 INNER PRODUCTS
definitions.text: returns a number measuring how aligned they are, and from which length and angle can be defined.

definitions.title: 11.1 CARTESIAN COORDINATE SYSTEMS, POINTS AND DISTANCE
definitions.text: is a list of coordinates; a curve or surface is the set of points whose coordinates satisfy an equation. 2D: point (x, y) in R^2. 3D: point (x, y, z) in R^3, with three mutually perpendicular axes (right-handed system).

definitions.title: 14.1 PARAMETRIC EQUATIONS
definitions.text: functions of a PARAMETER t (often time): x = x(t), y = y(t). As t increases, the point (x(t), y(t)) traces the curve. Advantages: curves that fail the vertical-line test (circles), direction of travel, speed.

definitions.title: 27.1 ALGORITHMS AND COMPUTABILITY
definitions.text: Not every well-posed question can be answered by a computer program, no matter how much time or memory we have. Computability theory studies exactly what CAN and CANNOT be computed. This is different from efficiency (complexity theory, Module 17), which asks how FAST something can be computed.

definitions.title: Module 29: MEASURES OF CENTRAL TENDENCY
definitions.text: A measure of central tendency answers: "What is a typical or central value of this data?" Mean, median and mode are three different answers to that question, and they can disagree. Which is appropriate depends on the shape of the data and what you want to know.

definitions.title: Module 31: MEASURES OF DISPERSION
definitions.text: Two datasets can have the same mean but be very different: test scores all near 70 versus scores spread from 20 to 100. Measures of dispersion (spread, variability) quantify how far values typically lie from each other or from the center.

definitions.title: Module 32: CORRELATION
definitions.text: Correlation measures how consistently two variables move together: when one is above its average, is the other usually above (positive), usually below (negative), or unrelated?

definitions.title: Module 33: PROBABILITY FOUNDATIONS
definitions.text: Probability is a number between 0 and 1 that measures how likely an uncertain outcome is. 0 means impossible, 1 means certain. It gives a consistent language for reasoning about uncertainty, which is the basis of statistics and machine learning.

definitions.title: 35.1 RANDOM VARIABLES: DISCRETE AND CONTINUOUS
definitions.text: A random variable turns the uncertain outcome of an experiment into a NUMBER, so that we can use algebra and calculus on it. "The number of heads in 10 tosses", "tomorrow's temperature", "the time until the next customer" are random variables.

definitions.title: Module 37: SAMPLING AND ESTIMATION
definitions.text: We rarely observe everyone. We observe a SAMPLE and use it to learn about the whole POPULATION. Statistical inference is the science of doing this honestly: quantifying how far the sample result may be from the truth, and how that error shrinks as the sample grows.

definitions.title: Module 38: PARAMETER ESTIMATION
definitions.text: We believe the data come from a distribution family (normal, Bernoulli, exponential) with unknown parameters. Parameter estimation chooses parameter values that make the model fit the observed data. Two classic recipes: match moments (method of moments) or choose the parameter that makes the observed data most probable (maximum likelihood).

definitions.title: Module 39: HYPOTHESIS TESTING
definitions.text: A hypothesis test is a structured way to ask: "Is what I observed in my sample surprising enough, if nothing special were going on, that I should doubt that 'nothing special' explanation?" It is proof by probabilistic contradiction: assume the boring explanation (the null), see how unlikely the data would be under it, and reject it if the data would be too surprising.

definitions.title: Module 40: LINEAR REGRESSION
definitions.text: Regression models how the AVERAGE value of an outcome y changes with one or more predictors x. Linear regression assumes the average changes in a straight-line (linear) way and finds the line (or plane) that fits the data best in the least-squares sense. It is the workhorse of statistics and the foundation of many machine learning methods.

definitions.title: Module 42: DATA SELECTION AND FILTERING
definitions.text: Most analysis starts with choosing WHICH rows and columns to look at. Every selection defines a SUBSET of the data; every statistic you compute afterwards describes THAT subset, not necessarily the population you began with. Filtering is therefore a statistical decision, not just a technical step.

definitions.title: Module 43: OPTIMIZATION ALGORITHMS
definitions.text: Training almost every machine-learning model means finding parameters that make a score as good as possible: the smallest error, the largest likelihood. Optimization is the mathematics of "find the input that makes this function as small (or large) as possible". Often no formula gives the answer, so we search step by step, using the slope of the function (derivatives, Modules 3 and 12) to decide which way to move.

definitions.title: 44.3 SPLITTING CRITERIA: GINI IMPURITY, ENTROPY, INFORMATION GAIN
definitions.text: measure is 0 for a pure node and largest for a perfectly mixed node. The best split is the one that produces the purest children (on average).

definitions.title: Module 45: RANDOM FORESTS
definitions.text: One decision tree is unstable: a small change in the data can change it a lot. But if you grow MANY different trees and let them vote, the individual mistakes tend to cancel out: the "wisdom of crowds". A random forest makes the trees different by giving each its own random resample of the data and by letting each split see only a random subset of the features.

definitions.title: Module 47: MODEL TUNING
definitions.text: Most models have "knobs" that you must set BEFORE training: tree depth, the strength of regularization, the number of neighbors. Model tuning is the search for good knob settings. The danger is that, by trying many settings and keeping the best score, you fool yourself about how good the model really is. The whole module is about searching efficiently and reporting honestly.
